speakeroldname: Mr. David Barrett (Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca) moved:
speechtext:
That this House calls upon the government to avoid a worsening of the social and economic hardship caused by the Canada-United States Free Hade Agreement by withdrawing from the current trade negotiations between the United States, Mexico and Canada.
He said: Madam Speaker, I regret it was necessary for my party to move this particular motion, but along with that regret is the awareness that it is absolutely essential that we go on record again against the consequences and the very principle of the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement, with the addition of Canada potentially sitting at the table with Mexico.
It is important to give a quick overview of what has happened as a consequence of the free trade agreement, what has happened statistically, economically, and frankly, what has happened politically. This House lost a staunch ally in the argument against the free trade agreement when the former leader of the Liberal Party stepped down and was replaced by its present leader. The Liberal Party has now softened its opposition to the free trade agreement. It has vacated its role in serious questioning about the Mexico-Canada-U.S. connection.
Reading the minority report submitted by the Liberal member on the committee one sees the typical Liberal response as the party gets closer to power. Free trade with Mexico is necessary, but not necessarily free trade. I wanted to put that on the record at the outset to prick the conscience of the Official Opposition and make it
understand it has a responsibility to participate in this House.
What nonsense.

I know some think that party historically has no conscience. Perhaps the party could be seen that way, but I feel individual members are rankling in discomfort over the fact that they have been dragged into a very neutral position on this issue.
Now I will address my comments to the government. I do not expect the government to fall today on reflection of what I have to say, but if it was serious and really concerned about the Canadian people, it would admit in the face of overwhelming evidence that their economic policies-with the free trade agreement being the apple of its eye-are the cause and the reason for our suffering so much economic hardship in a Canadian-made recession in this country today.
I recall sitting in the committee when we had the good fortune of having the Minister for International Trade appear before it. During the questioning in the committee I, along with the member for Kitchener, asked the minister clearly: "Can the minister state specifically how many jobs have been created by the free trade agreement?" He could not name one specific job, but in his defence, in response to the member for Kitchener, he said: "Give it a year". That was early last spring. He has had the time but still has not documented one single job that has been created by the free trade agreement.
Another year.

Another year, God save this country if we have another year in which we are allowed to follow the path of being totally taken into the United States orbit through this free trade agreement.
I recall that the Prime Minister made a statement immediately after taking office in 1984. He said, and I quote: "Give us 20 years and you will not recognize this country". This statement was incorrect, if not outright false. It has only taken from 1984 to 1991, seven years, for us to almost not recognize this country. The destruction of health care, the destruction of hospital insurance,

March 15, 1991

the destruction of national institutions, all Liberal programs which were forced in minority governments by NDP or CCF minorities, social democratic policies that were accepted by Tories and Liberals as a means of sewing the fabric of this nation together. All of them have been at risk.
Furthermore, in other areas of a mixed economy that were developed by consensus in this country, we have seen a gradual erosion of the things that are necessary, VIA Rail, CBC, transfer payments, Petro-Canada; all long term. Every single instrument that we agreed to in a consensus with former Conservative governments and Liberal administrations, and with the support of the Canadian people, to develop an indigenous mixed economy that gave us some foundation for maintaining a Canadian identity.
What are the facts? One hundred and fifty-two thousand Canadian jobs have been lost. I want to refer specifically to what some of the proponents of the free trade agreement were telling this country in supporting the government's position: 152,000 jobs have been lost.
Oh, oh.

I speak for myself and I wish the minister would speak for himself instead of for the President of the United States and for Carla Hills in the United States. Carla Hills tells the minister what tune to dance to. He is a very poor dancer but he makes an excellent try.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext: What a windbag.

That is no way to talk to the minister. I think it is shocking that the member behind the minister would call the minister a windbag. I think it is unparliamentary and I ask the member to withdraw it. I know they have internal cabinet problems but this is going too far.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order, the hon. minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I was referring to the hon. member who is speaking. If we unleash this kind of rhetoric on the prairies this summer, we would have the biggest wind and the biggest drought in the history of the prairies. Fortunately the wind is only going to be in the House.

I do not know under what part of Beauchesne that point of order is, but if the member wishes to defend himself and his cruel attack on the minister in that manner, so be it. I would never call the minister a windbag. I let the evidence stand for itself.
I want to go further by saying that in the food and beverage industry we were told we were going to have 6,400 jobs created by 1998. After two years, in that industry alone, we have lost 30,000 jobs.
Forestry employment was projected to remain constant over 10 years. In only the first two years of free trade there has been a 15 per cent decline in the number of jobs, a total of 11,000 lost. The government projected that the wood industry would grow by 2,000 jobs. After two years there has been a loss of 32,000 jobs. This goes on and on and on and still there is no explanation from the minister or the government, to all Canadians, the specific jobs that he claims has been created.
Far be it for me to quote back the minister's words, but sometimes it is necessary. I do not do this to be mean or cruel or to hurt the minister's feelings.
We would never suspect that.

I know you would not suspect that, but it is necessary sometimes to refer to Hansard, as embarrassing as it may be, to remind the ministers of some of the statements they made.
The member for Kitchener kept on persisting, in a meeting with a committee, asking the minister to produce evidence of jobs. He said: "Have any of those jobs been made public today, i.e. the number of jobs and the new investment?" "No, sir" said Mr. Shannon. Mr. Crosbie: "I have not seen any." Mr. Reimer: "How soon do you think we might see some?" Mr. Shannon: "In my view, it is probably too soon to make much sense of what there is, as I indicated to you." I then said: "Well, if you cannot tell us a list of jobs that have been created, could you make a list of the jobs that have been lost?" Others have done that, very clearly.
Your own member, Mr. Reimer, a profound, thoughtful member from Kitchener, who I last understood was a Tory, was the one who was asking these questions, not me. To insult your own member is a problem. I can take it, but to have your own member being rebuffed this way
March 15, 1991

is shocking and the Canadian people should understand this.
I want to refer to a specific statement made by a man who I have yet to meet. He was a cabinet minister in this House who, as I understand, ran afoul with some of the behaviour patterns that are expected to be normal for members of this Chamber and he came into disrepute. I refer, of course, to the hon. Sinclair Stevens. I want to refer to a statement that the former minister made since leaving politics. Remember, members, when an hon. minister makes a statement, we must take him at his word. It may put a lump in your throat, a loss of sub-electricity in the cell brains that you operate with, but you must take the statement.
Mr. Sinclair Stevens said, in early December: "Secret deal to boost the dollar. That part of the ingredient in the free trade agreement was to get the Canadian dollar up." He recounted a conversation he had with Mr. Baldrige, now departed. Of course, in speaking to Mr. Baldrige, Mr. Sinclair Stevens said that there was acknowledgement of a deal on the dollar. Mr. Baldrige is no longer alive and cannot recount his part of that conversation. The Minister of Finance has denied that any such deal took place and everybody has run from the issue. I asked the research department of the Library if we could get in touch with Mr. Baldrige and it is even outside of their ability to be able to do that.
But we have some other methods of contact around this issue beyond the use of a leftover Liberal ouija-board. What I want to refer to is the mysterious coincidence that exists about the date within which Mr. Stevens said this deal was made on the dollar, the time Mr. Stevens said Mr. Baldrige said the deal was on, and put that timeframe into what has happened to the Canadian dollar. An amazing coincidence.
In December of 1985, a conversation was confirmed to have taken place by one of the participants, Mr. Stevens. In early 1986 and up until the present time, the grasp on the value of the Canadian dollar goes up, up, up, up. There was a little spurt just before the last election when they got nervous. Maybe the Liberals would win. That faltered, and it is still going on.
Supply
There is no rational fiscal reason why the Canadian dollar should be so high, except that it logically fits to benefit the United States in this free trade agreement. This government has not used it as a fiscal instrument to protect us.
I could not talk to Mr. Baldrige; I talked to his staff. It is very easy to do. You phone to the United States. I want to thank the Speaker for allowing us to use the telephones. I phoned the people on the committee and, lo and behold, I spoke to Mr. Franklin C. Pfeiffer, Jr. of the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade. He was very vague on the question, but he said he would send me a copy of the committee hearings. So I have here the hearings before the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade of the House of Representatives, 100th Congress, Second Session, February 9, 26, 29, March 1, 11, 25 in the year of Our Lord 1988.
Throughout all of these hearings, the U. S. Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Baker, was asked about the Canadian dollar being too low because as we enter a free trade agreement it would be an impediment. What could be done to get the Canadian dollar up? What is the government's policy on getting the Canadian dollar up?
I want to tell you of a strange phenomenon. I have marked four specific areas of this report where Mr. Baker was asked by members of the committee about the Canadian dollar, and in every single instance he said to the committee member: "Mr. Member, I will talk to you privately about this issue". In four instances in front of the committee, when he answered every single question, when it came to the Canadian dollar he said: "I will talk to you privately about this deal".
The deal is off.
Secret deals.

Now, someone of a suspicious mind would say that if the government's former minister would lose her briefing papers-and I am very careful when I describe that, Madam Speaker, her briefing papers- when the government cannot produce its own documents as to its position, when Sinclair Stevens makes this serious allegation and it is brushed aside, and when it is raised in U.S. committees, they are told they will be given a private briefing by the U.S. Secretary of State,

March 15, 1991
Supply
someone of a suspicious mind would say Sinclair Stevens knew what the hell he was talking about.
Since I have a very brief time, and that is tragic, I must now devote my time to the next step of the free trade agreement, expanding it to the Mexico connection.
This House had a committee set up under the able, capable, competent chairpersonship of the hon. member for Don Valley West. There was outstanding leadership on that committee, and profound thoughtfulness in setting up the meetings, but he was confined by a limited budget to having hearings only here in Ottawa. He was told too, and the rest of us on the committee were told that we should not worry, the government would not make a decision about participating in the Mexican talks until the committee did its work.
Don Valley West.
Don Valley West. Well, Don Valley went west when it came to this government, given some support to the committee's chairman and the promise to the committee chairman.
It has gone south.

Gone south is even more appropriate. One day before the committee was to start its hearings, the government announced that it was on the road toward getting going on the free trade talks.
During the course of the committee hearings, I frequently asked, politely, in deference to the skill of the committee chairman, for detailed reports done by this government before it entered on any such major undertaking on behalf of the Canadian people. We have seen not one single document produced by this government showing independent research evaluating the pros and cons of the Mexico-U.S. connection. There is a minor little paper from the Department of Science and Technology, but for a major undertaking by the Canadian government, no valid research has been tabled.
We were promised a labour studies project. It is still to be released, so the good work of that committee was for naught. We were being used as a bluff hand in a game in which the cards were already counted up. They are all in the United States hands.
One of the critical arguments we used in that debate and in this Chamber was: What is the impact of us competing in Mexico against low wages, no health or safety standards, poor environmental conditions and the minister's answer in this House? The the Prime Minister's answer is: Are we opposed to giving the opportunity for a Third World country to lift itself up?
I felt humbled by that devastating attack, but I kept it up. I thought someone in the government would have the sense and the responsibility to ask those questions before we embarked upon the free trade discussions.
Did anybody in this government ask? No. Was there an outcry from some of the backbenchers? No. Was there confusion from the Liberals? Yes. I want to refer to how the American politicians take their responsibility. Even though there is an impression left that somehow everything is on track down there, let me show how they go about these things.
I ask the minister in response if he will stand up and accuse the Americans of being anti-Third World. Here is a copy of a letter sent to the President of the United States dated March 7, 1991 signed by Mr. Lloyd Bentsen, chairman of the finance committee and Mr. Dan Rosten-kowski, chairman of the ways and means, the Congress and the Senate. I will read one paragraph alone to make the point that is necessary: "A number of members of Congress have expressed concern about the proposed extension of fast track authority, particularly as it applies to the proposed free trade agreement with Mexico. They have identified a number of legitimate concerns that in our judgment should be addressed in a meaningful way before Congress considers the extension of a fast track authority. Specific concerns include the following: the disparity between the two countries in the adequacy and the enforcement of environmental standards; health and safety standards; and workers rights."
Here is the United States of America that is expounding the new world order that this government subscribes to, questioning what is going on in these areas in Mexico and this government has not uttered a peep about the very same questions.
The reality is that the Americans are deeply concerned, as we are, about the social issues, and also the wage and working conditions that would destroy job
March 15, 1991

opportunities for Canadian workers, men and women, from coast to coast in this country.
I know I have only one minute left in such a short timeframe and such a catalogue of material. But let me tell you this, Madam Speaker. The New Democratic Party has catalogued the devastation of the free trade agreement. It has been consistent in its opposition to the free trade agreement. It is now consistent in us not participating in talks with Mexico and is the only party on record that says: "If we should gain power, we will give the six months' notice to abrogate the treaty because it has been a betrayal of Canadian working people".

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question.
During the course of his comments, which of course were very high in rhetoric and short in any real factual content, he claimed that 152,000 jobs had been lost as a result of the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement.
I have in my hands the document called CLC Today, December/January, 1991. It says that the CLC estimates that 226,000 jobs have been lost because of the free trade agreement, whereas the hon. gentleman is saying 152,000 jobs have been lost. This is a considerable difference: 74,000 jobs.
I am wondering why it is that the CLC are greater exaggerators even than the hon. gentleman.
I note in the document that the CLC gives us a whole list of what they say are the job losses: Albright and Wilson Americas, the phosphorus plant at Long Harbour, Newfoundland, 290 jobs gone. I happen to know, since it is in my district, that it had absolutely nothing to do with the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. It had nothing to do with marketing. It had to do with the age and the technological capacity of that plant compared to other plants they have in the world. It had no connection to the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement.
CBC in Toronto, 500 jobs. What did that have to do with the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement? Broadcasting was not covered in the agreement at all, or crown corporations. Clearwater Fine Foods in Port Mouton,
Supply
Nova Scotia, 150 jobs listed. That plant closed because of a scarcity of fish. Then they list National Sea Products in Canso. What did that have to do with the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement? That was because of a scarcity of fish. Molson-Carling across Canada, 1,400 jobs. Beer did not come under the free trade agreement at all. I can give you more examples. VIA Rail: what did VIA Rail have to do with the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement?
Is the member admitting that this CLC document is a piece of fiction, totally inaccurate, viciously ignorant, carelessly ignorant, a Maude Barlow kind of document, the product of a mind seized by fantasy? Does he agree that this is the case and therefore has reduced his estimate by 76,000 jobs compared to this tendentious piece of fiction from the CLC? "Season's Greetings" they say from the Tory government. I say that the CLC, Madam Carr, and the rest of them should apologize for trying to foist on the people of this country such a piece of fraudulent material as they have issued.
I am glad to see the hon. gentleman is correcting them today, and I hope he will come right out and say that the CLC in its fanatical opposition to the free trade agreement has gone too far in publishing such a document.
Does the hon. gentleman agree that at least 76,000 of those jobs are purely fictional?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the minister for effectively deflecting the fact that he cannot produce one single job on the record, not the CLC, not Dave Barrett, but on the record showing that it has been created by the free trade agreement.
As to the document, I don't have to defend the CLC. I ask the minister to attack my figures. Furthermore, I have not brought in the business community's figures that it uses in support of this government: the Canadian Conference of Businessmen, or that other ragtag outfit, or the banks that shell out money for this government, the bank that has admitted that it has given money to this government because it is more to the specific policy. If you want to get in the trades on support, I will tell you this -and I say this proudly-that I would rather have the working men and women of Canada supporting my position than the right-wing business community of this country.

March 15, 1991
Supply
I want to repeat my question. Why is it that non-captives of the CLC-Mr. Bentsen, who was a vice-presidential candidate, and Mr. Rostenkowski-are moved to write to their President asking for guarantees while this government has even denied that such requests are necessary? Why is it that an American senator and American members of the House of Representatives have the courage to raise these questions, but when they are raised in this House they are attacked by that minister who views all criticism as a personal insult?
I have never attempted to insult the minister personally. His own record does that better than anything I can do. I have been a sympathetic friend of the minister. I have been waiting for him to come to his senses, but I think it is now beyond his ken. There is a call for that member to go back to Newfoundland and lead the Tory party. They are already in oblivion. What possible help could he give them in that course?
The questions are clearly focused; the questions are clearly stated.
This government has not produced research. It has not produced documents showing that all the warm bodies they have in bureaucracies have put their mind to this question, but they have spent $25 million on the Spicer commission, on airy-fairy searches for basic problems of this country which have more to do with economics than anything else.
The greatest threat to the province of Quebec is not the internal divisions in this Chamber, but the free trade agreement which will ultimately lead to the loss of its economic sovereignty. I challenge the members from Quebec and the rest of Canada to understand that the greatest threat to the survival of any potential nation- sovereign or member of a confederation-is the economic sovereignty they can determine within their own borders. When that is lost you do not have a country, and this country is becoming a lap poodle to the United States and is losing its great heritage as an independent sovereign nation with some control of its own economic destiny.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca on his witty speech in the House today. I agree it is a shame he did not get more time to speak to us this morning. I think he
would be great on the Improv programs we see on U.S. TV or on the Johnny Carson Show. It is a relief to have someone who can start the morning with so much humour and wake up the Tories with the kind of comments he just made.
I admire his sense of humour, and I admire him for what he has done for the parliamentary channel. I am sure that this morning, everybody in Canada is saying: Let's get rid of the Spicer Commission and ask Barrett to tour the country and talk to us about Third World countries and Tories, and especially about the excellent programs introduced by the Liberal Party when it was in power.
I like the hon. member's sense of humour and I admire him for it. It is really too bad that his opposite number in this respect, the minister responsible for free trade agreements with the most powerful country in the world or one of the Third World countries- The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca never said which of the three was from the Third World. He missed an opportunity there!
So again, my congratulations, and it would be nice to hear some more from Mr. Barrett and enjoy his humour for the rest of the morning.

Madam Speaker, I deliberately focused in seriousness on the government's position in response to questions in this House about the Third World. I was shocked, and still am, at the facetiousness with which the government answered those valid questions about the impact on our economy of having a low-wage partner in a free trade agreement.
I want to point out again that regardless of the party you belong to, it is imperative that we protect and defend those people who send us to this Chamber. It is not good enough to put ourselves in a position without asking serious questions about it. It is not good enough to place ourselves in a position of being at the mercy of a low-wage partner, particularly when the other partner is asking these questions and we are not. I am ashamed of the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure as always to have the opportunity to speak in this House, even though the motion before us is a silly and jejune motion. It calls upon the government to avoid a worsening of the social and economic hardship caused by the Canada-U.S. Free

March 15, 1991

Trade Agreement. There has not been any social or economic hardship caused by that agreement.
It then goes on to say: "by withdrawing from the current trade negotiations between the United States, Mexico and Canada", when there are no current trade negotiations between the three. This is a matter which is before the U.S. Congress now to decide whether or not it will give fast track authority for such a negotiation. No negotiations are yet started.
I want to correct something the hon. member who introduced the motion said. He said he was tiying to prick the conscience of the Official Opposition. Well, how can you prick what isn't there? To prick something you first have to find it. I have never noticed, and I do not think anyone else in this Chamber has ever noticed the Official Opposition having a conscience. He started out already in attempting to do the impossible.
When I knew you, you were a Liberal.

That is why I happen to know they have no conscience. That is why I left them, to look for a party that had a conscience.
The motion is basically about free trade. I want to give a quotation from Thomas Paine in 1791. Two hundred years ago in The Rights of Man he said:
The prosperity of any commercial nation is regulated by the
prosperity of the rest. If they are poor, she cannot be rich, and her
condition, be it what it may, is an index of the height of the
commercial trade in other nations.
In other words, we are all dependent upon one another if we are to be prosperous in this world. That was recognized even 200 years ago. We cannot be prosperous if the people who surround us are poor.
That quotation alone completely knocks on its head the feeble attempts of the New Democratic Party to oppose a negotiation between the U.S., Canada and Mexico. We all know that Mexico is not as wealthy a nation as ours at the present time, but does that mean that we should, even in our own self-interest, refuse to trade with it, refuse to have anything to do with it because it suffers from lower wages at the moment than we do?
Supply
Is that the New Democratic Party philosophy, the party that used to be the party of support for the undeveloped countries of the world, for those who had been dispossessed, for those struggling to make their way up?
Now they are members of the party of the status quo, because they bob their heads whenever the organized labour movement of Canada tells them to bob their heads. They have deserted their principles. They no longer want to help the dispossessed, the poor of the world; they just want to help the fat cats in the Canadian Labour Congress to try to maintain a position where there must be walls of protection to keep them in their present status, and to hell with the rest of the world.
That is not the philosophy of our party. The NDP supports the status quo. We support change that is needed for the future together with the business community, which today are the revolutionaries. The revolutionaries of our society are the business and industrial people who realize that we have to compete with the world and change.
I would now like to give another quotation. I am raising this debate to too high a level for these hon. gentlemen to understand. Here is what T. B. Macaulay, the famous historian, said in 1824 in Mitford's History of Greece:
Free trade, one of the greatest blessings which a government can
confer on a people, is, in almost every country, unpopular.
That is what Macaulay observed in 1824, and it is correct. Any government that tries to lead a country into freer trade must know it is not a popular move to make, because it is a longer term move. It is something that is going to be good for the country in the longer term. The ignorant and those who do not want to see and those who are beholden and dependent upon certain selfish interests will oppose it and make it appear that any change in the status quo is going to somehow be damaging to the ordinary person. That is why it is not popular.
It only becomes popular when you stick to your guns and keep explaining what the benefits of free trade or freer trade are, which we intend to do. We have all kinds of independent opinion that supports what we have been doing.

March 15, 1991
Supply
For example, the national financial columnist, Diane Francis, said in Maclean's for November 12, 1990:
The lingering debate over free trade is irrelevant, as is the battle against the goods and services tax. Opponents of both are practitioners of ostrich economics, the tendency of persons with a low economic IQ to simply stick their heads in the sand. The GST and free trade initiatives, whether bilateral, trilateral or multilateral, are essential policies in sync with the irreversible post-war trend towards a global economy.
She goes on to say:
Free trade is profound historical trend which is as immutable as gravity. The debate of the 1990s is not whether free trade is a good idea or not: the debate should centre on how to adjust, how to improve strengths, cushion dislocations and find new niches.
Canada is already so far along in this process of interdependence that our standard of living and future depend strictly upon how astute and non-protectionist we are. Up to one third of Canadian jobs are directly or indirectly dependent upon trade with other countries.
Then she points out that we collectively owe more than $230 billion offshore, giving us the dubious distinction of having one of the highest levels of foreign indebtedness per capita in the industrialized world, almost $9,000 per person. She says:
Canada's challenge is to figure out how to earn more hard currency from foreigners and how to motivate workers to work harder. If not, our standard of living, already on the decline, will fall further in the 1990s. Of course, people do not want to hear such messages and would rather vote for politicians who espouse ostrich economics.
The largest ostrich of them all just spoke ahead of me. She concludes:
The world hurtles towards one global economy, whether we like it or not.
The NDP is like King Canute telling the tide to stay out, defying the tide. King Canute Barrett sits there. The world is hurtling toward one global economy and poor little fat Dave saying: "No, no, no, we are not going to hurtle toward one global economy.* Here in Canada somehow we are going to keep things all together. We are going to depend on our own spavines in a market of 26 million people and we are going to protect ourselves into prosperity. Whereas, what would really happen is we would obliterate ourselves altogether.
The world hurtles toward one global economy whether the NDP likes or not. You are not even an infinitesimal speck on the beach with the tide rolling in over you.
That is what Diane Francis said. On January 14, 1991, Diane Francis said this in Maclean's as well:
Critics of the free trade deal are intellectually dishonest. The facts
show that Canadians have prospered under the agreement.
You will have to read the article. I do not have the time to read this whole article today. When we look at some impartial observer, that is the kind of report we get, not the fearmongering and fiction that the New Democratic Party imparts or the Liberal party spreads.
Part of the Liberal Party is inculcated by a bacillus, a bacilli that has come from the New Democratic Party. It controls your foreign policy section. It used to control your trade section. Now you have a trade critic who is fighting against this infection from the NDP, tiying to adopt some sensible trade policy. There are even Liberals who have supported the U.S.-Canada-Mexico negotiations. Former leadership candidate, Sheila Copps, said that Canada has to protect its interests.
Oh, oh.

"I am not sure that we should become a negotiating partner, but I think we should make sure we know what is going on". That member at least wants to know what is going on. She says: "If we are not anywhere near the table, clearly we are not going to be in a position to monitor that". This is a woman showing a modicum of common sense for the first time in her history.
Then metro Toronto MP Kaplan, we are sorry to hear he is not going to run in the next election. He did not have a chance anyway. He said: "Canada should try and get the largest role that we can in the talks to protect our interests".
They are in disagreement with the former honourable Mr. Axworthy. Perhaps he is still an honourable; hon. member Axworthy, now the foreign policy critic who turns faint when he hears anyone mention the word U.S. We are not even to mention the word U.S.
March 15, 1991

To come back to the main theme of my remarks, we can look at practically any independent study. Here is a study done by the C. D. Howe Institute, Competitiveness in the 1990s. What does it recommend?
It recommends the following:
Recommendation 2: Canada should be a full and active participant in the U.S.-Mexico free trade negotiations.
Recommendation 3: Canada should continue to press for the enhancement of secure access and bilateral trade negotiations with the United States under the FTA.
I do not have time to refer to more of its statements. These are independent research bodies, not long-winded labour politicians like poor Bob White, Shirley Carr and this crew who think that somehow they have got to kowtow to their followers and pretend that somehow Canada can protect itself and cut itself off from the rest of the world.
In The Gazette of Montreal for February 27: "Free trade agreement pays off for Canada", a report of a speech by Ambassador Derek Burney, who sets out-
Oh, oh.

Oh, they laugh. Whenever they hear about facts they laugh in the NDP. They do not know how to deal with facts. Here is one of the facts that Derek Burney put forward:
Fact number three is that Canada's trade performance is one bright spot in an otherwise sombre economic outlook. The OECD has pointed out that "Canada's strength in international trade has cushioned the country from a more debilitating recession. The free trade agreement, far from opening the floodgates to job-destroying U.S. imports, is presiding over a substantial increase in our trade surplus with the United States -$17.4 billion for 1990 as opposed to $14.2 billion in 1988. The value of total Canadian exports to the United States has increased nearly $8 billion, or 7.5 per cent, since 1988 to a total of $110.3 billion in 1990."
That just happens to be a fact. How could this be if Canada has been devastated and we have lost hundreds of thousands of jobs? How is it that we are exporting more to the United States of America than we ever did if we have lost hundreds of thousands of jobs due to this agreement?
They never deal with these facts. We never hear them deal with the facts. All we have is fiction from Shirley
Supply
Carr, Bob White and the seven dwarfs, and all the rest of them. Somebody should deal with these facts:
Fact number four is that the investment picture in Canada is even more impressive-we have moved from a net direct investment outflow of $7.3 billion in 1988 to a net inflow of almost $1 billion in the first three quarters of 1990-a remarkable turnaround-since the free trade agreement -
What creates jobs? Investment creates jobs. Instead of having an outflow of $7.3 billion as we had in 1988, losing jobs, we had a net inflow of $1 billion in 1990 helping to create jobs here in Canada. These are facts, but we never hear facts dealt with by the hon. personages opposite.
Then let us look at the Canada West Foundation report that just came out in February. This studies objectively the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Under conclusions it states:
Contrary to prevailing perception-Canada has significantly expanded its exports of end products by a net increase of over $4.0 billion while imports of end products from the U.S. declined by $600 million.
Despite poor conditions economically there are increases in "exports of machinery, equipment, electronics, aerospace and others". We made our "gains in high-tech and capital-intensive industries rather than selling off our resources".
That is what the Canada West Foundation reported. It has no bias. It is not controlled by any political party. It is just doing a job for the west, an independent job, and those are some of the conclusions that it has come to.
If I had the time I could go through and show that conclusion after conclusion knocks the NDP on the head and the silly statements that it makes. The Maude Barlow party, any party that spouts the same nonsense as Maude Barlow, my God, should be ashamed of itself. It should go hide its head.
Looking at the Canada West Foundation report, the interesting things about these patterns, it states on page 7:
- provincial-U.S. trade in the West and Atlantic regions and to a lesser extent in Quebec, has grown substantially higher than Ontario-U.S. trade which dominated Canada-U.S. trade in the post WWII period.
I do not have the time to read it all to you, but you have not got the patience to listen to it either.

March 15, 1991
Supply
The Royal Bank of Canada Econoscope, February 1991, concludes that the FTA has been very beneficial for Canada and that we should enter into a Canada- U.S.-Mexico free trade agreement.
Dr. Neufeld, an executive vice-president of the Royal Bank, made a speech in Washington to the National Economists Club and concluded after two years of the Canada-U.S. FTA that:
Our own study of the functioning of the Canada-U.S. Free Hade Agreement released today finds that the current recession has little to do with the Agreement; that some sectors are benefiting from the Agreement; that the dispute settling mechanism has contributed to a more orderly review of trade disputes; that precise reasons for some plant closings in Canada and shifts to the U.S. are not clear; that there are areas where Canada and the U.S. must take action to improve the Agreement; but that major policy difficulties in Canada lie not with trade but with fiscal deficits, cost increases, interprovincial trade barriers, federal-provincial tax system disharmony, and low productivity. So I see nothing in the functioning of the Canada-U.S. FTA so far that would argue against further evolution in North American Free Hade.
These are the remarks of an outside observer, not a politician out to appeal to the prejudices and the emotions of people they should be better serving by giving them the facts and the truth.
On page 4 of the same speech:
The North American free trade area would encompass a population of 360 million, which is larger than the European Community and three times as large as the lapanese domestic market. It would constitute combining the labour abundant and capital scarce region of Mexico with the technologically advanced industry and demographically aging population of Canada and the U.S. It is a strategic fit.
Read the serious material and see why we are doing it. We are not doing this because we think it is going to be instantly popular in Canada. We know we have a whole series of vicious people who do not care about the future of Canada who are going to be attacking this looking for short-term gain. Any person in this country who studies this objectively, knowledgeable people, commend the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. They recommend that we go on to negotiate a North American free trade agreement.
The hon. NDP member talked about jobs, jobs, jobs. I can give him examples of tens of thousands of jobs. Are
you listening? No, you are not listening; you are gazing blankly into the space above your head.
Here is one example of jobs. "Windsor to get high-tech steel mill. International group, led by Dofasco Steel, plans a $240 million investment. One thousand new jobs by 1993." If you want jobs, brother, I will show you jobs. "Bayer to invest up to $165 million in Canada after a Polysar purchase". On and on it goes with examples of expansions and new investments in Canada.
I recommend the Royal Bank of Canada Econoscope study.
Diane Francis says: "Free trade gets a ringing endorsement and that is the Canada way". "Trade deal benefits Manitoba", a report says. Then we have an analysis of the Mexico negotiations by Fred Blaser in The Financial Post: "Canada will give as good as we get."
The experts know that we can compete with Mexico. The experts know that low wages do not determine whether you are competitive or not. They know it depends on science and technology. They know it depends on transportation systems and education systems and a whole set of other factors, not just wages which are less than 20 per cent of the cost of goods normally.
Because I do not have a huge amount of time left, here is another thing about jobs. Proctor and Gamble gives free trade thumbs up:
We've become substantially more efficient in the last two years
and clearly we now have more jobs in our Canadian plants than we
would have had without the agreement.
After two years Mr. Dave Elliot, an executive at Proctor and Gamble, in the December 21, 1990 Evening Telegram, says: "We have become more efficient and clearly we now have more jobs in our Canadian plants than we would have had without the agreement".
Is the hon. member listening to that? Does anybody see the hon. member listening? Has he heard a word?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Unfortunately I must interrupt the hon. minister. The time has expired.
It being 11 o'clock a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 35, the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

subsubtopic: TELETHON ON BEHALF OF MR. ROBERT CORBEIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, next Sunday I will be taking part in a telethon to help Mr. Robert Corbeil, a resident of the municipality of Mont-Rolland in my riding. After Mr. Corbeil became a quadraplegic as result of an unfortunate accident, residents of Mont-Rolland started a campaign to help Mr. Corbeil and his family.
Madam Speaker, today everybody in Laurentides knows about Mr. Corbeil's case. I want to take this opportunity to pay tribute to all my constituents who have shown an incredible spirit of community and compassion by getting involved in various projects to help Mr. Corbeil. The telethon is one of those projects, and I urge all residents to give generously.

Madam Speaker, the more we hear from farm organizations about the Farm Income Protection Act, the more we are being told that this legislation is not completely what farm groups were expecting and promised.
Farm leaders who thought they were being consulted expressed shock and disappointment that this legislation does not contain measures enshrining the producer's share of premiums, and there is no reference in the bill to the principle of equity for producers of different commodities in different regions of Canada.
We on this side of the House join the agrifood industry in Canada in calling upon the government to make crucial amendments to the bill to protect in the long run a vital sector of the Canadian economy, that of the agrifood industry.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in the Journal de Montreal, we read: Blais:
According to Pierre Blais,
Edmonston has been engaging in misleading advertising.
It is false to say that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs supports corporations at the expense of consumers.
According to the newspaper:
The member for Bellechasse wanted to remind Mr. Edmonston, the NDP consumer critic, that he often asks CCC to intervene in matters that are not under the department's jurisdiction. He mentioned gas prices and explained that setting gas prices was not the responsibility of CCC. Furthermore, hidden guarantees for automobiles were a provincial, not a federal responsibility.
Madam Speaker, the article goes on to say:
The Minister explained that in many consumer areas, responsibility was shared by both levels of government, but considering the present constitutional context, the provinces would not look kindly on the federal government trespassing in an area for which they had responsibility.
This is a clear message to the NDP.

Madam Speaker, once again on behalf of Atlantic Canadians, especially Newfoundlanders, I want to register deep concern and outright protest over the destructive overfishing by the European Community vessels.
Figures just released show that for 1990, European Community vessels are estimated to have caught 76,000 tonnes of groundfish stocks. This is five times over the quota of 15,377 tonnes set by the members of North Atlantic Fisheries Organization.
In addition, despite a NAPO moratorium on the harvesting of northern cod, the European Community set a unilateral quota of 32,000 tonnes. It is clear that in 1990, as they have in the past six years, foreign vessels have disregarded the quotas they set for themselves, and more importantly, they are getting away with it.

March 15, 1991
The people in the fishing industry are fed up with statement after statement. It is imperative that this government develop a system with teeth to end the overfishing and to protect the livelihoods of fisherper-sons in the Atlantic region.

Madam Speaker, a comprehensive child care plan was the promise of the Tories on the campaign trail in 1984 and again in 1988.
Child care groups across this country anticipated, after almost seven years, that this government would be announcing child care initiatives in this budget. Nothing. There is no new money for child care, in spite of a promise in the 1984 election, in spite of a promise in the 1988 election and in spite of a number of promises in this House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in response to my questions.
He said that in the life of this Parliament we would have child care. The same minister said that we should look at child care as an economic and a social instrument.
What did Canadian families get? They got a response from the Minister of Health and Welfare saying that the money would have to come from a combination of federal financial reserves and reallocation of other program commitments.
Is this the government's commitment to affordable, accessible child care? Is this what working families can expect; we will pay for child care with money we steal from other social programs? Some promise.

Madam Speaker, March 15 has been declared International Consumers' Rights Day, under the theme: protect consumer rights.
Founded in 1960 by five groups from the United States, Great Britain, Australia, Belgium and the Netherlands, today the International Organization of Consumers Unions has 181 member organizations in 64 countries, on all continents. The organization tries to find solutions to problems, international in scope, relating to consumer products such as pharmaceuticals, pesticides and tobacco.
The message of the International Organization of Consumers Unions is especially important for developing countries and countries in Eastern Europe that are now setting up market economies in which consumers have a major role to play.
In Canada, Madam Speaker, consumers are protected by framework legislation, and especially by a market that is sensitive to consumer needs.


1848 REVOLUTION

Madam Speaker, I stand here today to address the issue of the Reform Party and their agricultural policy, or rather their lack thereof.
My concern is that Mr. Manning and his splinter reformers have not the slightest idea of the complexities of the agrifood industry. Mr. Manning admits he is a management consultant from Edmonton with no connection to the soil.
Uncertain about the complexities of the farm situation, Mr. Manning acknowledges that his agricultural ideas might not work. Mr. Manning has refused three invitations to appear before the finance committee and perhaps if he were to receive an invitation to appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture, he likely would refuse that invitation as well.
What are his ideas? Nobody, including Mr. Manning, knows. If Mr. Manning and the Reform Party hope to be a credible force in the next federal election, someone had better come up with a solid agricultural policy, or any policy for that matter, one that the agrifood producers can look at and closely evaluate on its merits or lack thereof.
Therefore, I ask: where is your agriculture policy, Mr. Manning? Where is the wheat? Mr. Manning, where is the beef?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance is making the world's poor shoulder the burden of his economic mismanagement.
After cuts in 1989 and a 5 per cent cap in 1990, the minister decided in the February budget to reduce the cap on overseas development assistance, to 3 per cent in 1992-93 and following years. Although this will save Canada $262 million next year alone, the results for the Third World will be harsh.
In its recent review of member's foreign aid programs, the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development expressed, "regret" at the "significant decline in Canadian overseas development assistance". The OECD report concluded that: "Canada's real commitment to its announced aid target must be in question."
Tory times are not only hard times for Canadians, they are also hard times for the poor and impoverished of this world who look to Canada for her humanitarian help and leadership. I urge the minister to read the OECD report and significantly increase, not cap, Canada's ODA.

Madam Speaker, Canadians are fascinated by the new Crow rate. The Governor of the Bank of Canada preaches wage restraint as a miracle cure to fight inflation, but in practice he accepts yet another generous salary increase from the Conservative government on the day before wages are frozen for secretaries, clerks, and other federal employees.
Crow's salary has increased 69 per cent over five years. Crow says high salaries at the bank are necessary to retain staff. Then why is it that Crow's counterpart in the U.S. gets paid $100,000 less than Governor Crow, and the U.S. chairman is doing a much better job of earning his salary too. Unemployment in the U.S. is just 6.5 per cent, compared to the 10.2 per cent which Wilson and Crow have forced on Canadians. The U.S. federal bank rate is 4 percentage points lower than in Canada.
Canadians can neither afford the hypocrisy nor the destructive economic policies of this disastrous duo, Wilson and Crow.
Madam Speaker, the Governor's pay rate is one Crow benefit that Canadians would be happy to see cut.

Madam Speaker, the outbreak of the PVY-N potato virus has caused much concern in Atlantic Canada.

March 15, 1991
Oral Questions
The federal and provincial governments and the Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick potato boards have just announced the implementation of an eradication plan that will eliminate PVY-N and ensure that the normal trade patterns can be resumed.
In addition, Agriculture Canada has begun negotiations with the United States and has already succeeded in reducing U.S. import restrictions.
Madam Speaker, as I have indicated to the House in the past, the Canadian agricultural industry depends upon the export of top quality crops not only to the United States but to the world.
By having the various levels of government and industry work together, we can ensure the eradication of this virus and the continued success of Canadian agriculture.

Madam Speaker, Montreal-said the late Jean Marchand-is the motor of Quebec's economy. Montreal, my city, is crying our for help because of the disastrous impact of unemployment. Montreal has broken the gloomy record set by St. John's, Newfoundland, the unemployment champion. According to an article that appeared in La Presse on Thursday, March 14, the fact that 180,000 workers are unemployed does not seem to impress the minister responsible for Montreal and especially for East Montreal. The minister keeps recalling the situation under the Liberals, but he should realize that the Liberals were judged by the Canadian people in 1984 and 1988. The people of Montreal don't want to know what the Liberals did or did not do but what the Minister of Labour, the minister responsible for Montreal and especially for East Montreal, intends to ask the government in the way of emergency measures.

Madam Speaker, last night on The Journal the member for Duvernay made a statement in relation to our aboriginal people that we in
the New Democratic Party, and I am sure most Canadians, find offensive.
The statement was both racist and bigoted. When this type of statement is made by any Canadian it must be challenged. When it is made by a member of Parliament is it unforgivable. At a time when Canadian national unity is at stake and there is a need to promote greater understanding and tolerance, this type of statement is particularly regrettable.
We would call upon the member to immediately apologize to aboriginal peoples and to all Canadians. We call upon the government to dissociate itself from this member and his statement.

Madam Speaker, on February 26 this year, the Minister of Finance brought down his budget for 1991-92. The aim of this Budget is first of all to control inflation and to achieve economic recovery. These measures are necessary to stabilize prices, which will have a positive impact on economic recovery. The measures to control wage settlements in our latest Budget are intended as an example to be followed by all levels of government and the private sector. These measures will make it possible to bring interest rates down even further, to a level compatible with genuine economic recovery, and will improve the standard of living of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.

On February 15, 1990, the House of Commons of the Parliament of Canada unanimously passed the following motion:
That this House reaffirm its commitment to support, protect and promote linguistic duality in Canada, as reflected by this House in the Constitution Amendment, 1987 and the Official Languages Act 1988.
March 15, 1991

I ask the Acting Prime Minister under whose authority were unelected officials meeting behind closed doors last week at Meech Lake to discuss possible changes to the Official Languages Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, many people were in attendance at the meeting to which the hon. Acting Leader of the Opposition refers, including a number of academics, who made a number of suggestions concerning the future of this country. Obviously, the government is willing to listen to as many suggestions as possible. That is why we have the Spicer commission. We will listen to the Beaudoin-Edwards committee. We will listen to recommendations or suggestions that may come from members of this House.
I would like to tell my hon. friend that our commitment to the Official Languages Act is full and complete and total.

Madam Speaker, my second question is for the same minister. On February 15, 1990, the following resolution was unanimously adopted: "That this House reaffirm its commitment to support, protect and promote linguistic duality in Canada, as reflected by this House in the Constitution Amendment, 1987 and the Official Languages Act, 1988."
I direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. Last week, under what authority did he put on the table one of the basic issues in Canada, namely our bilingual character, one of the fundamental traits of our country? And under what authority did non-elected public servants put that question on the table?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
First, Madam Speaker, I want to tell my hon. friend that the Government of Canada did not put anything on the table during that Meech Lake meeting. There have been consultations with various groups, including academics, and certain suggestions were made. Naturally the Government of Canada is quite prepared to listen carefully to all suggestions, be they from academics, from the various commissions struck by the federal and provincial governments, or from members of this House. But I
Oral Questions
should like to say to my colleague that at any time the Government of Canada-

-is fully committed to the Official Languages Act.

Madam Speaker, there is a fundamental contradiction in what the Acting Prime Minister is saying today. On the one hand he is restating the government's support for the Official Languages Act, and on the other hand he says that he is prepared to listen to any particular issue. This is another example-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: What's the matter with that?

-of where the closed-door process at Meech Lake is not going to work.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister state today that there is a fundamental characteristic of this country, and that fundamental characteristic includes our bilingual nature and in particular the protection of language minorities wherever they live in Canada? This item is not negotiable and it should not be put on the table behind closed doors at Meech Lake.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as has been made abundantly clear, that question was not put on the table by the government. It is not an open question for this government. The commitment of this government to official bilingualism is clear, constant, and continues.
Let me ask the Acting Leader of the Opposition if she would provide the House of Commons with a list of those questions on which she believes it is improper for Canadians to express their views.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment.
In the Green Plan, the minister stated, and I quote: "-the federal government has required environmental impact assessments for all proposals coming before the Cabinet for decision. A statement of the environmental implications of new policies and programs will be

March 15, 1991
Oral Questions
made public at the time that the Cabinet initiative is announced".
Last week, in response to a question on free trade with Mexico, his colleague the Minister for International Trade rejected the Green Plan flatly when he said that he was not bound by that clause.
Here is my question: Does the Minister of the Environment agree with his colleague?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the policy is clear. What was stated in the Green Plan and approved by the Cabinet is that every document submitted to the Cabinet had to contain a section dealing with the environmental implications of the proposed decision.
This policy was implemented and will be enforced. As far as the requirements set as a result of this decision are concerned, we were to release the information contained in that section, or a summary of it, to the Standing Committee of the House on the Environment.

Madam Speaker, let us be very clear that the minister has contradicted his colleague.
The Minister for International Trade has issued a direct challenge to this minister. Last week, the Minister for International Trade stated that the environmental consequences related to trade should not be subject for negotiation within the context of the Mexican free trade agreement.
Two days ago, Mr. William Riley, Director of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, stated the contrary. He stated that we should have separate environmental agreements on some matters, yes. But he went on to say that where the environment and trade impact on each other, he accepted the linkage of the two within the Mexican free trade agreement. That is only common sense.
Which side is the Minister of the Environment on, that of common sense or that of the Minister for International Trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no dichotomy because common sense and the Minister for International Trade are one and the same thing.
Oh, oh.

The hon. gentleman certainly has not quoted me accurately. I have said that the U.S.-Canada-Mexico negotiation on a free trade agreement is a trade negotiation.
If there are concerns about environmental matters, then they can be dealt with in a parallel negotiation. They will not likely be dealt with in a trade negotiation. This is the same position as Mrs. Hills has taken in the United States.
Use some common sense.
They ask questions, and then you hear this mumbling and muttering while you are trying to respond, Madam Speaker. I am a person of some shyness, and this frightens me.
Oh, oh.

Madam Speaker, just as we did in the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement, we negotiated an environmental agreement, signed just two days ago.
If it is necessary and if it looks like there is a lot of interest, we will negotiate on a parallel track with respect to the environment.
By the way, we already have an environmental agreement with Mexico that was signed by the Prime Minister a year ago. We are working with Mexico on the environmental issues.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This is a supplementary to the question of the hon. leader of the opposition.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs tells us that he and his government support this country's Official Languages Act. Considering that a representative of his party approached our party with a proposition to abolish
March 15, 1991

Oral Questions
the parliamentary committee on official languages, can the minister explain why, if he supports official languages in this country, we have a proposition by the government of Canada to abolish the parliamentary committee on official languages?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not personally aware of my colleague making the representations the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville alleges were made. However, I can assure him of our full, complete and total support to the Official Languages Act.
I want to thank him and his party for supporting the motion we introduced in this House on February 15, 1990.

Madam Speaker, another question in terms of national unity in this country that is very, very important, and this again goes to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Acting Prime Minister. Last June, about 10 days before the Meech Lake Accord collapsed, the Prime Minister made a proposal to aboriginal people of this country, and included about six points, including the establishment of a royal commission on aboriginal rights and a greater definition of the treaty rights of aboriginal people.
Also, a comment was made last night by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, and I quote, "It's like the Indians, they do not respect our laws, they do not respect the Constitution, but they want to have the money".
In light of that comment by the member for Duvemay, will the minister first of all dissociate the government from that comment about Indian people and second, would it now move to implement the promises made to aboriginal people in the middle of June of last year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the question of the statement carried on The Journal, a statement by our colleague from Duvemay, the hon. member will know that the member issued a statement this morning and I will quote, if I might, Madam Speaker, a brief reference from that.

"The hon. member explained that he was thinking of the behaviour of certain warriors during the crisis at Oka last summer when he said those words."

It was consequently, Madam Speaker, a statement, as I understand it, more limited than is suggested by the hon. member.
Look at the transcript.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will nonetheless take a look at the whole transcript. The hon. member suggests we take a look. She has been on The Journal and she will know that sometimes not each of her priceless words is recorded on the television program. We will look at the transcript and see if any further action remains to be taken.
With respect to consultations with the aboriginal people, of course it is the intention of the government to find appropriate and effective ways in which those consultations can proceed.

I want to pursue this point with the Acting Prime Minister.
Last June the Prime Minister made a commitment to doing six different items for the aboriginal people, including a better definition of treaty rights to be enshrined in the Constitution; a recognition of aboriginal people as a fundamental characteristic of this country; and most important, the establishment of a fully fledged royal commission on aboriginal rights of the stature of the commission on bilingualism many, many years ago.
I would like to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether or not he thinks that the proper way to start this important round of constitutional studies we are about to enter into would be to fulfil these promises made to the aboriginal people, the first nations of this country. Is that not the proper way to begin this very, very important round of constitutional talks that are so vital to all the people of this country? Is that not the proper signal to send?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has, I am sure, been following some of the questions of his leader in the House. He will know that she has referred, among other things, to the interest expressed again most recently by aboriginal leaders to be involved in discussions. She referred, I believe yesterday in the House of Commons,

March 15, 1991
Oral Questions
to a letter sent by the National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, a letter of which she had a copy but which had not, at that time, been received or seen by the Prime Minister.
I now have a copy of that letter and we naturally are going to be responding to that letter in a way that encourages the fullest possible involvement of aboriginal people, including aboriginal leaders in discussions of Canada's Constitution.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, I address my question to the Acting Prime Minister. The finance minister's home town of Toronto is not, as the government perceives, the fat-cat city, but rather a tale of two cities with a chronic unemployment undercurrent.
Given that Toronto unemployment is reaching double digits in which 194,000 people were unemployed in February, up 25,000 from January and that since 1989,
75,000	jobs were lost in Toronto, more than half in the manufacturing sector, will the Acting Prime Minister acknowledge the devastating impact that government policies have had on the Toronto economy and when will the government provide the federal leadership necessary to kick-start an indispensable engine of the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the city of Toronto and surrounding areas commonly referred to as the Golden Horseshoe, probably saw unprecedented growth in the period 1984 up to early 1990. Jobs were plentiful. The unemployment rate was very, very low. During this period of time, unemployment has risen, but it is still the lowest unemployment rate in this country.
From reports coming out of Toronto, we are seeing some turns in the economy which we expected. It is still not what we would like it to be and we probably will not come out of it until the summer. But I can say that with housing sales having doubled over the last month, there
is activity again in Toronto, especially with first-time home buyers, I am informed. Interest rates have dropped over 4 per cent. They dropped again slightly yesterday, continuing their downward trend. We feel very confident that Toronto and in fact all regions of this country will benefit from the activities and the policies of this government.

Madam Speaker, the only turns happening in Toronto are going downward. Again, I go back to the Acting Prime Minister.
The true tale of Toronto is that there are 123,000 people on the welfare rolls. The Toronto housing and construction industries are in a nosedive. Nine hundred Toronto businesses went bankrupt last month and
110,000	Torontonians feed themselves thanks to the the good graces of the 200 food banks operating in that city.
Why is the government's federal budget so void of employment initiatives that are so desperately needed by real Canadians facing real problems? When are we going to put Canadians back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
I take a look at some of the headlines coming out of Toronto: "Resales Boom", "Relief as Toronto home sales double". Economic activity is starting to come back in the Toronto area. These are from Toronto papers. I understand the concern of the hon. member.
We are concerned about the unemployed as well. But we remember very well a previous government that tried to throw money at problems and did not solve any problems. It did not solve the problem in any way, shape or form.
What this government wants is the economy back on track, permanent full-time jobs, not part-time jobs with money thrown at them because that does not solve the problem. The problems can be solved by sticking to the proposals brought forward by the Minister of Finance in his very well accepted budget of February.
Our economy will be back moving again early in the summer and by 1992 the hon. member will up singing the praises of this government and the economy in Toronto.
March 15, 1991

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Health or, perhaps, to whom it may concern.
Financial analysts estimate that $5 billion invested in better day care, before and after school programs, and in higher incomes and more community support for single parents will result in 187,000 children remaining in school and receiving adequate education.
Does the minister not think this $5 billion is a worth-while investment for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is, of course, concerned with the poverty rate and the children in Canada. That is why since we have come into office over 300,000 children who were under the poverty line before are not any longer. So we have made progress.
With regard to the second part of the question which refers to children staying in school and the amounts of money that we put into those programs, I suggest to my hon. friend that he take a look at one of our recent initiatives which was the Stay In School initiative, whereby the federal government will provide over the next four years an amount of $300 million to try to decrease the horrible drop-out rate of children, especially poor children, in this country.
We are proud of the initiatives of this government and I am very proud of the initiatives of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

Mr. Speaker, it is not enough. There is a great deal of difference between $300 million and $5 billion.
My supplementary is for the same minister. The Senate's recent report Children In Poverty-Toward a Better Future states that those 187,000 Canadians would contribute $23 billion to the Canadian economy over 20 years. That means an additional $7 billion plus income taxes and over $1 billion in sales taxes.
Oral Questions
Given those numbers, why does the minister persist in relegating Canadian families to the tragic cycle of poverty? Why continue to cut programs that generate wealth and opportunities?

I would like to refer my hon. friend to one statistic which I think is very meaningful; that is the total of our three main transfer payments to the provinces- the EPF, equalization payments and the CAP program.
When we came into office in 1984, the amount was $22 billion. I would like to tell my hon. friend that now the federal government is transferring to the provinces over $36 billion this year. That is an increase of approximately 6.9 annually per cent since we have been in office. So the increase in transfer payments has been much higher to the provinces than the increase in the budget of the federal government.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister who will recall a few months ago that the Prime Minister announced a war on drugs and asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to play a critical in drug enforcement in Canada. He also will know that the RCMP is one of Canada's most famous symbols, both nationally and internationally.
I would also say to my hon. friend that the RCMP is one of the institutions that unifies Canada at this very, very difficult moment.
My question to the Acting Prime Minister is this: In 16 days the federal government will abandon its traditional role of support for the RCMP in terms of cutting back on the amount of money it provides for its support.
Can the Acting Prime Minister explain why, at this very critical moment in our history, the federal government would be abandoning its support for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):

Madam Speaker, I think all of us here will agree with part of what my hon. friend has said; the importance and

March 15, 1991

the good reputation of the RCMP, the famous reputation of the RCMP.

There is one reality on the other hand that has to be taken into consideration, and that is the cost of the RCMP to serve in those provinces, territories or municipalities; and that is under a contract that was signed 10 years ago to which there are some adjustments that are necessary. We made an offer in September 1989 to start discussions to renew, not abandon, the contracts. My supplementary question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister who comes from western Canada where the impact will be greatest and where in fact millions and millions of dollars will be added to the local taxpayers in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia.
Does he and his colleagues support at this very critical time loading up the local taxpayers with additional policing costs and as a result requiring many local municipalities to look to their own policing options and perhaps beginning the demise of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in western Canada?
Does he and his colleagues support this abandoning of the RCMP in terms of funding at this very critical moment in Canadian history?

Madam Speaker, I think it is very important. My hon. colleague should be a little bit less partisan on this issue, because what is occurring is that there are services provided to eight provinces, two territories, and I believe 190 municipalities across the land, except in Quebec and Ontario.
The contract was signed in 1981 for a 10-year period provided that in 1990, at the date we are right now, the split between the provinces and the federal government would be 70 per cent supported by the provinces and 30 per cent paid by the Government of Canada and all taxpayers across the country.
