speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I begin by expressing to my colleagues who are critics for other parties in this House my regret that there was a brief delay in my transmitting a copy to them of the statement I intend to make. As members of the House will know, this has been a long week and I apologize to them for the 10 or 15 minute delay in delivering that statement.
Over the last seven and a half months, the Kuwait crisis has riveted our attention and engaged much of our debate.
Today Kuwait is again a free country, though deeply scarred by its ordeal.
I visited free Kuwait five days ago. I raised over the Canadian Embassy there, the flag our diplomats so reluctantly took down when they were forced by lack of food and water to leave on October 19.
I wish now to report to the House on that trip which began, quite deliberately, with a call on the Secretary-General of the United Nations in New York and which took me to Jordan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Iran as well as Kuwait and the United States. I met with leaders of those countries and with the foreign ministers of Egypt and of Italy, and with leading Palestinians from the Occupied Territories.
In Jordan, I visited the headquarters of United Nations agencies working with the casualties and the consequences of the conflict. The Canadian government is contributing to many of their activities, but I want to draw the attention of the House and of Canadians to the United Nations Children's Fund operated by UNICEF for humanitarian assistance for the children who are victims of the conflict. The government has contributed an additional $550,000 to that fund and I hope individual Canadians might make their own contribution to that special Gulf Disaster Relief Appeal, organized by UNICEF Canada to provide medical and humanitarian assistance to mothers and children suffering the effects of that conflict.
My purpose was to look beyond the liberation of Kuwait to the issues this crisis has underscored. The fundamental problems remain, but there are now new possibilities which need to be nurtured.
My interest, as the foreign minister of Canada, was everywhere understood and welcomed. As a member of the coalition of countries who, through the United Nations, came to the aid of Kuwait, Canada's commitment to the liberation of Kuwait was clear.
But Canada also represents a lifetime of commitment to the United Nations. My primary mission was to try to ensure that that the sort of world consensus which emerged to free Kuwait be further mobilized to prevent such aggression in the future, and to strengthen the chances of enduring peace and security. That is the first lesson of this crisis.
There are other lessons. As the Prime Minister said on February 18, one such lesson is that reckless transfers of arms must come to an end. Canada's commitment and record on arms control entitle us to place this item high on the world's agenda. I reviewed with leaders of other countries of some of our proposals to reduce the flow and risk of arms.
Progress, of course, will be slow, but everyone I met in the immediate aftermath of a decade of conflict in the gulf acknowledged the need to address this problem, and to do so practically and persistently. The House should know that in some gulf countries the immediate reflex may be to buy new arms to deal with threats they believe will continue. That underlines the need for countries like Canada to advance proposals like those the Prime Minister has set forth.
But for real peace and security to emerge and for arms transfers to diminish, the underlying causes of tension have to be resolved. These tensions, many of which relate to enduring disputes between Israel and her neighbours, were a major topic of my discussions.
Madam Speaker, no one in the Middle East has forgotten a single moment of history, and there is a lot of history to overcome. There is now, however, an opportu-
March 15, 1991

Routine Proceedings
nity-now, but not for long. The world must not lose that opportunity.

Many of us have said that the recent events have changed the Middle East forever. Canada's purpose has been to make those changes for the better-to strengthen the United Nations, to increase the control of arms and to reduce the risk of war, and to resolve the tensions at the root of insecurity in the Middle East.
I congratulated Mr. Perez de Cuellar, on behalf of the people of Canada, for his resolution during this crisis. He thanked Canada for our support, and believed that Canada had set an example for other states by our determination to settle this crisis through the United Nations. He informed me that the United Nations is poised to police the separation of forces, once an official request is received from the Government of Kuwait.
He also urged us to try to heal some of the wounds of this crisis by helping leaders with whom Canada has close ties-such as King Hussein of Jordan. He was concerned about the Palestinians whose leadership had been so criticized, but whose right represent a continuing challenge to the reputation for fairness and effectiveness of the United Nations. Indeed, this issue dominated many of my subsequent discussions.
On my way to the region, I also met with Secretary of State Baker, just before he embarked on his own tour. He shared our view that there is a psychological moment of opportunity to be seized on the agenda for arms control. His immediate concerns were with the arrangements for regional security which would enable the United States to withdraw its ground forces from the theatre and bring the troops home.
Even as we spoke, of course, the Foreign Ministers of the Gulf Co-operation Council were meeting in Damascus with the Foreign Ministers of Syria and Egypt to reach agreement on the stationing of Syrian and Egyptian ground forces in Kuwait, to replace Coalition ground forces, once a definitive ceasefire with Iraq was arranged.

Madam Speaker, I believed that my trip to the area should begin with the government of Kuwait. The Emir of Kuwait was still in Taif, in Saudi Arabia, where he had
spent the occupation. His appreciation for Canada's contribution to the liberation of Kuwait was heartfelt. The Emir was deeply concerned at the damage to his people and to his state. Plans are already beginning for the massive reconstruction of Kuwait and I welcomed the clear assurances that the expertise of Canadian companies will enjoy opportunities commensurate with the important role Canada played in liberating Kuwait.
The senseless damage to Kuwait must be seen to be believed. Across the limitless desert landscape burn innumerable fires, each set deliberately with powerful charges of high explosives. Downtown, on the waterfront, are burned-out building after building, looted store after store, museums, homes, things of value or merit, trashed. This was not war damage; this city was put to the torch in the last 48 hours of occupation.
For the Kuwaitis, the ending of sanctions against Iraq is therefore a major problem. Should oil exports again earn revenues for Iraq when Kuwait remains crippled? On the other hand, Iraq itself is badly damaged and needs to finance its own recovery. One idea being explored by countries of the region is the dedication of a proportion of Iraq's oil revenues to repair the damage Saddam Hussein has done.
Much will depend on what kind of regime survives in Iraq. Saddam Hussein is now being challenged by his own people. But through the force of arms and oppression he can cling to power. As long as he does, the countries of the region will be wary of his designs and will want continued sanctions on anything enabling him to rebuild his armies.
In Kuwait, there is a mood calling for change in the way the country governs itself. The government says it is anxious to open up the regime, to institute more democracy. I encouraged that development and urged that particular care be taken to allow the reintegration of Palestinian residents of Kuwait, many of whom, most of whom, were intensely loyal to Kuwait.
Almost everyone with whom I met indicated that the Palestinian problem is the key issue to be resolved in the region. The answer will have to be found in greater security for all states of the area. The issue has three essential elements which all must be respected. They are the security of the state of Israel, the rights of the Palestinians and territory.

March 15, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Sequence and relationship-which goes first, and what is tied to what-could consume thought, discussion and negotiation for years. Meanwhile, were that to occur, the despair of the refugee camps would find more radical expression and the arms race would go on.
I sought in my discussions in Jordan, in Syria, in Israel, and in the home of a leading Palestinian, Faisal Husseini, to promote appreciation of the need to build confidence in the collective ability of states and peoples to live together in acceptance and security. Eventually, a healthier state of mind can be built. There is not a lot of time. The countries and peoples concerned could make gestures, take initiatives, not of a kind which bear upon their fundamental security interests, but which build up a habit of working together. That is the message I left with all those with whom I met.
Could not Lebanon be the theatre of such co-operative action to further strengthen the authority of the government of Lebanon?
Could some progress be made among the states and parties on water projects?
Can peoples see their welfare in terms of a shared and more harmonious future, instead of a bitterly divided past?
Madam Speaker, it is not clear that they can. But that is the best way to build trust.
Much time in this discussion is devoted to technique, to whether it should be an international conference, at the United Nations or not at the United Nations, or whether it should be separate bilateral negotiations, and whether discussion between the Palestinians and the Israelis should be part of that or separate, and, in any case, who should represent the Palestinians, and so on.
On that last point, Canada can only agree with the Secretary-General of the United Nations; the Palestinians should be represented by the organizations or representatives they choose. Our distaste for the support for Saddam Hussein by the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization should not disqualify Palestinians from coming to their conclusions on what we have always said was fundamental; their right to choose their own leadership in the search for realization of their legitimate rights.
As I said in Jerusalem to the Prime Minister of Israel, we are among the closest friends of that country.
Canada will not let Israel be put at risk. As the Prime Minister of Canada said on February 8, and as President Bush said a week ago, there is no security in geography.
I also went to Iran. My meeting with President Rafsanjani was productive. Of course, we discussed problems-human rights and hostages for example. But we did so in a way which gave me hope that Canada can work well with Iran.
These countries are all neighbours of Iraq. They are not disinterested in the outcome of the current uprising there. Indeed, Syria, Saudi Arabia and Iran have brought together in Lebanon the leaders of the various groups representing the masses of people wishing to be done with Saddam Hussein's tyranny, not just the Shiite majority in the south, not just the Kurdish minority in the north, but others as well. We have always said that the future of Iraq is up to the Iraqis. I encouraged other states in the region not to intervene.
I have been encouraged by all the leaders I spoke with. They want a durable peace in the region. They are however not yet ready to move beyond the liberation of Kuwait to address the age-old problems on which they have been so long divided, except with wariness and with distrust. But move they must. Or the arms race will spiral, and the United Nations will lose the lustre of its concerted action to liberate Kuwait. That would be our common loss.
By its nature, this is an interim report to the House, and I will be coming back to the standing committee as early as next week.
My conversations last week gave me a more direct understanding of attitudes in a region whose conflicts are deep and dangerous. They reinforced Canada's ability to play a constructive role in calming those conflicts and in using the end of a war to begin a real peace. I know that all members of this House share our commitment to that goal.
As our ships head home from the gulf, proud of our contribution to one victory, we are seeking now to address the sources of that conflict. Last July no one foresaw the invasion of Kuwait; no one foresaw the unprecedented response of the United Nations. We cannot foresee the developments of the next several

months except to say that they offer a real chance to resolve the most intractable conflict the world knows, and it is in Canada's interest to make the most of that opportunity.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs for his statement on the Persian Gulf crisis and the search for peace, and indeed the role that Canada has played. I found it very interesting as I am sure all members of the House did.
On behalf of the Liberal caucus, I would like to respond to the hon. minister's statement.

Like all Canadians, the Liberal caucus is happy and relieved that the war in the Persian Gulf ended so quickly. The primary objective of the United Nations, supported by all Canadians to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait and restore this country's sovereignty was achieved.

The Liberal caucus commends all members of the Canadian Armed Forces, especially those stationed in the gulf region, for their professionalism and their dedication in carrying out their duties. I also want to register our sincere gratitude to the members of their families for their understanding, their dedication, and indeed their steadfast support in these difficult times. We are all thankful that no Canadian lives were lost.
The end of the war marks only the beginning of a much more difficult challenge facing the international community, the challenge of reconstruction, development and stabilization in the Middle East, as the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs has just explained.
The destructive impact of war has been very severe. The economies of Iraq and Kuwait have been virtually destroyed. Those of other states in the region such as Jordan and Egypt have been significantly hurt. Scud missile attacks on Israel destroyed hundreds of housing units. The waters and coastlines of the Persian Gulf are blackened by oil, and the skies over Kuwait and surrounding lands have been darkened by hundreds of oil well fires. Thousands of civilians are homeless and sick; the danger of epidemics is very real. The situation is desperate.
Routine Proceedings
Estimates of the cost of all the necessary reconstruction, environmental cleanup and humanitarian assistance in the region range well into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

Madam Speaker, the war also had a negative impact on many, mostly Third World countries that were not belligerents but suffered as a result of rising oil prices and dwindling export markets.

Moreover, some of the root causes of tension in the region still must be addressed. These include the lack of adequate regional security arrangements, continuing economic and wealth disparities between the various states, problems of democratization and human rights, religious fundamentalism and territorial claims and disputes affecting states and people such as Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Israel and the Palestinians.
The impact of the war on the United Nations must also be carefully considered. The members of the coalition, including Canada, have lauded the United Nations for demonstrating the capacity to act on behalf of the international community to halt aggression. We speak of the new world order.
The Liberal caucus agrees there is potential for an important new status for the United Nations, but we are convinced that this requires the United Nations and its agencies to be actively and centrally involved in the search for peace in the Middle East.
The Liberal caucus has always supported the collective security provisions of the United Nations charter. We have always accepted that the use of force to uphold the United Nations principles may be necessary, but as a last resort.
That being said, we recognize that there have been valid concerns expressed about the potentially negative impact on the United Nations, and I say the potentially negative impact on the United Nations, of its willingness to endorse war before other options to resolve the gulf crisis had clearly proven inadequate.
There are valid concerns about the relegation of the Security Council to the sidelines once war had started. There are also valid concerns that the five permanent members of the Security Council, who agreed on the

March 15, 1991
Routine Proceedings
issue, may well be disposed to disagree on other issues of international peace and security which might prevent the Security Council from playing a role in the future.
We believe that Canada must be vigorous in ensuring that these concerns are addressed.

Madam Speaker, I would now like to address the search for peace and Canada's role in this respect. The Liberal caucus feels that Canadians should urge their government to play an active role in meeting reconstruction needs in the short term and seeking peace in the long term, in the Near and Middle East. They should also urge the government to encourage the UN to act consistently and consider restructuring the UN to that end.

The government has laid out some preliminary thoughts on this role. The minister has just expanded on these interesting thoughts in the context of his trip to the Middle East. I am sure it must have been a very tiring experience.
I must commend the minister on looking so fresh after what must have been an exhausting experience for him. We welcome him back to the House.
Bravo.

We particularly support the government's interest in humanitarian and other economic assistance, economic cleanup assistance and controls over arms sales to the region.
We note, however, that the visit of President Bush this week to Ottawa, which displayed its undeniable successes, has clearly illustrated the sharp differences of opinion between the Government of Canada and the United States over the issue of controlling conventional arms transfers.
It is sobering to know that since 1961, $1.6 trillion has been spent on arms in the Middle East. As well, I note that the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament recently estimated that the United States plans to sell weapons totalling $25 billion to the Middle East this year.
We urge the government to continue pushing hard on this issue. I note that the standing committee of the House on national defence and veterans affairs is studying this assiduously. We are hoping to come up with some suggestions on a non-partisan basis to the government, which may be able to present some rational and practical achievable ideas in this very difficult and hard to grasp issue which is so key to the downstream happenings in this area of conflict.
I recommend to the Secretary of State for of External Affairs that he undertake a special diplomatic effort to seek out support for reviving the idea of conventional arms transfer talks, first attempted in the late 1970s by the Carter administration.
Liberals believe further aspects of Canada's contribution to building a durable peace in the Middle East should be considered. The following is a series of possible initiatives that we offer and urge the government to support and promote. There are six of them.
First, the promotion of an important role for the United Nations and its member agencies in providing economic aid. The current scramble for reconstruction contracts in Kuwait has not yet been matched by a serious commitment to provide comprehensive aid to the countries of the gulf region hardest hit by the war.
Although a second Marshall Plan of sorts has been suggested by the Government of Canada among others, it would appear that little else is yet being done to co-ordinate an effective aid program that addresses not only reconstruction needs, but also those relating to health and disease prevention, environmental cleanup, food distribution, temporary shelter, management of refugees and some of the other needs.
One means of dealing with these myriad needs is to involve the United Nations and its member agencies which have responsibilities in various agencies requiring assistance. Such agencies include, among others, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the United Nations Development Program, the United Nations Environment Program, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the United Nations Disaster Relief Organization and the Food and Agricultural Organization.
An active role by the United Nations and those agencies could help to promote the United Nations legitimacy in the region.
March 15, 1991

The Liberal caucus urges the government to actively promote an initiative by the United Nations Secretary-General to increase the United Nations involvement in relief efforts for the peoples of the gulf region, stressing humanitarian aid and long-term economic aid. Canada could lead by example, earmarking specific funds it intended to contribute to the United Nations for this purpose.
Second, we would like to assist the Third World nations negatively affected by the gulf war. As we have heard this morning, many Third World economies have been severely hurt by higher oil prices and reduced exports due to the crisis in the gulf.
The Liberal caucus believes Canada could play an important role in mitigating this impact through efforts to encourage special assistance in various forms such as increased import quotas, debt relief, reduction measures and new financing.
The government's decision to cut back official development assistance once again in the 1991 budget unfortunately sends the wrong signal at the worst time.
The third initiative relates to peacekeeping and verification. I don't think anybody can deny that our participation in the war limits to some extent our involvement in a peacekeeping operation. We do have experience and we should draw upon that to assist in the organization of such an operation and in the larger task of maintaining the peace.
In our minds, there are two major needs to be met. The first is to provide a framework for conducting an interim border patrol pending the operation of the development of a more permanent regional security arrangement. The second is to develop mechanisms for verifying and monitoring possible agreements on controls over arms transfers and other security arrangements.
The Liberal caucus urges the government to promote a central role for the United Nations in contributing ideas, expertise and co-operation to meeting these needs. We could propose a scheme similar to that used at the time of the Korean War when the Security Council appointed a committee to plan and promote peacemaking and peacekeeping mechanisms.
Next there are confidence and security building measures. "A journey of a thousand miles must begin with a
Routine Proceedings
single step." This is an age-old statement and it has stood the test of time. There is a need to begin slowly building the foundations upon which new political and economic structures can be erected in the Middle East to bring a durable peace in the region. The Liberal caucus believes that Canada could encourage the creation or development of some of these building blocks.
For example, Canada should encourage the states in the region to consider increasing areas of mutual trade. Steps could be taken to encourage moderation and compromise among the countries of the region in the interests of seeking a durable peace. The government should encourage key Arab states to engage Israel in peace negotiations, leading to an end of their formal state of hostilities with that state and an end to the Arab boycott. They could also be asked to affirm Israel's rightful place as a member of the United Nations and support a repeal of the United Nations General Assembly resolution equating Zionism with racism.
The government could also encourage Israel to resume efforts to set up a peace process with Palestinians in the occupied territories as the first step toward achievement of a peace settlement which accords recognition to legitimate Palestinian political rights. We agree with the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs that this is a fine requirement.
The fifth initiative involves arms control and arms reductions, to which I spoke earlier. Security, especially for the heavily armed countries of the Middle East, cannot be achieved overnight or through a single event. The Mulroney government's call for a world summit on armaments, while laudable, is no substitute for real steps, however small, that are designed to reduce the likelihood of a military conflict. In fact, they should complement each other.
The Liberal caucus therefore believes that Canada should promote a series of specific arms control and arms reduction initiatives in pursuit of this goal. We should push for a rapid conclusion of a convention on chemical weapons and the strengthening of existing conventions on the use of weapons in war, both conventional and mass destruction. Effort should be put into restricting and prohibiting the transfer of these weapons and their components. Indeed, supplier nations, which include most prominently the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, should themselves be

March 15, 1991
Routine Proceedings
encouraged to tighten their export controls and to allow public disclosure of their military exports.
Canada must also place special emphasis on encouraging countries of the Middle East who have not signed the non-proliferation treaty to do so.
Finally the sixth initiative: a review of the security provisions of the United Nations charter. We all know that the charter is over 45 years old and the world has changed significantly. The use of peace and security provisions of the charter during the gulf crisis has been lauded, but legitimate questions were raised about their proper interpretation.
If the United Nations is to emerge as the chief custodian of a new world order and if chapter VII of the UN charter is to play a new and stronger role in enforcing decisions of the UN Security Council, as is our hope, we must ensure that the UN's mandate is fully understood and accepted.
The Liberal caucus therefore believes that it would be of great service to the community of nations if the Secretary-General were to initiate a comprehensive review of the necessary steps provided for conflict resolution under the charter to ensure their effective and consistent application.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As time has gone by, I have to seek unanimous consent of the House for the hon. member to continue. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, and I would like to thank my colleagues, especially the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do apologize but it is a very important subject. Again I thank my colleagues for their indulgence.
We note in this regard that the United Nations charter provides in chapter VI for a procedure under the authority of the Security Council to settle disputes before aggression occurs.
To our knowledge no attempt was made by the Security Council, which included Canada at the time, to address the Iraq-Kuwait border and oil dispute in the weeks and months before Iraq invaded Kuwait. Indeed, the record shows that Iraq began making threatening military gestures toward Kuwait several weeks before invading, yet no state saw fit to ask the Security Council to consider
chapter VI action. This lack of foresight should not be repeated.
By way of conclusion, the Liberal caucus, in putting forward the six points to the government, is convinced that if the United Nations is to emerge as a leading player in the management of international peace and security, it must be vigorous in promoting its role as an active participant in both the short and long term peace process in the Middle East. There is a window of opportunity there, and we should use it. Canada's position should be one of making every effort to sustain the United Nations in that enterprise.
We should therefore encourage the long-term changes the United Nations requires to become the agent of choice of the world community to lead the process of constructing and maintaining this new world order.

Madam Speaker, I wish to thank the House for the opportunity of commenting on the minister's remarks.
I want to say that I was taken aback at the modesty of the minister apologizing to the House for delaying his comments being made available to us 15 minutes late. I think the House owes the minister a vote of appreciation for so quickly coming back to the House after his arduous journey and presenting this report. It is a compliment to his commitment to the parliamentary system that in spite of the journeys he has been taking he saw fit to come to the House as quickly as possible and present us with this report. He should be commended for that.
I suppose we all do a great deal of thinking about these issues. We are free to decide the world's problems in the security of this wonderful country of Canada. However they are complex problems, and made even more complex by some of the actions we take when we think we are trying to solve them.
The minister has been profoundly open in expressing his opinions about what he perceives Canada's role could be, as a minister responsible to the Crown should be, and should be commended for that. I feel a sense of pride as a western Canadian, understanding that my colleague from Alberta also represents that region and that he plays an important part regionally in this government.
Having said the complimentary things, I must address myself now to the content. We have picked some strange partners in the region. While I listened intently to the comments of the minister, I am compelled to reflect

March 15, 1991

Routine Proceedings
essentially on one of his comments, and that was: "no will be necessary to confront some of those partners we one should forget history". But the question is: Have we allied ourselves to with the very serious problems we learned from it?	have in accepting their backgrounds.
Throughout the process of the coalition, and we are talking about results now, it is well-known that my party would have rather had a longer time with the sanctions. That argument is over, and gracefully it has been accepted as over I think in some elements of the United States as well here in Canada. Now we live with the consequences, and the question of learning with history as it is in front of us.
I put to the minister that we inherited an awful lot of baggage with President Assad of Syria. President Assad of Syria, who we picked up as an ally of necessity during this current crisis, does not come to the table with the kind of background that gives me or my party confidence that in the long run he might not even be a greater problem than Saddam Hussein.
Without giving a catalogue to the House of that particular leader's background, suffice it to say the nation that sacrificed most in terms of materiel and political prestige in this experience was the United States of America. It must be said that the United States of America has been the best friend of this country and we in turn are their best friend, but that gives us the right, too, to tell our best friends when we think they have bad breath.
One of the things that worries me about the United States of America and launching us into a compelling alliance in this experience is the fact that it has now embraced President Assad, the very same person who is directly responsible for the murder of those 200 U.S. marines in Lebanon. This must be said. I am not the minister. I do not have to be the diplomat but it must be said. We are dealing here with a very dangerous person who runs an autocratic government and who has demonstrated in the past that he has even a worse capacity than Saddam Hussein to deal with opponents and with enemies real or perceived. That alliance, because of his participation, is fraught with dangers.
I do not say this exclusively in terms of the United States, but I also say it as it relates to member states in the region, including perceived opponents such as Iran, which has gone through some amazing transformations in our public relations evaluation of who it is and what it is over the last six months. It is going to be difficult, but it
I do not know how a diplomat says to Assad: "We know who you are, where you came from, and we do not want to see that around any more". But that in effect is what I hope is said.
Second, I want to deal with the particular role of Jordan. I was particularly appreciative of the comments of the minister about not making a fast judgment on Jordan. I think that is essential, and I commend the minister for that.
I said on January 17, in my brief comments on the regional scene, that we should not rush to judge Jordan, that we will have a difference of opinion of where Jordan comes down in reality or in perception. The fact is Jordan must be a major player in the region and King Hussein must have the support of western nations in the fragile situation that he is in. We should not make judgments about a political response to populace clamouring on the street but understand that we have a role to play in maintaining that state as it is and as it evolves. It is not perfect.
The Saudis as well need to be gently nudged by a country such as ours-and our Prime Minister correctly suggested that the Saudis be allies of ours-that the fight was for human rights and against human rights violations by Iraq. The Saudis are also not very clean in terms of the same catalogue of definition that the Prime Minister used, that is Amnesty International, when he spoke to this House. The Saudis also have not a very good record with Amnesty International.
Dealing with Kuwait itself, if we pick up this morning's paper we discover that everything we said in terms of our definition of liberating a sovereign nation comes to a question about what we liberated in terms of loss of materiel and life and the consequences of that loss.
I will just use this one headline to illustrate my point from today's edition of The Globe and Mail: "Kuwaiti women struggle to tear off traditional chains". I would ask that the minister consider, on reflection, some subtle message perhaps to the Kuwaitis to understand that there were women in the Armed Forces who served in this country, there were women in that theatre who

March 15, 1991
Routine Proceedings
were prepared, on behalf of this country's commitment to the liberation of Kuwait, to risk their lives. I do not think it serves the long-term interests of women's commitment, equal with men, to risk their lives in a fight by the government and others for the liberation of a sovereign nation, to find out that they liberated an archaic system that does not recognize the rights of women. Just as an aside, also no votes for women.
I want to deal now with the arms issue. None of these things are said, by the way, as any criticism of the minister, and I mean that sincerely. I have the liberty of speaking on behalf of a third party which gives a lot of licence beyond the boundaries of diplomacy, and I recognize that.
I am impressed by the position taken by the government against the arms race, but I must reflect-and I do not mean this maliciously but sadly-on some of the facetious responses given to my colleagues by government members, not this minister, when questioned about ARMX and ARMX's role here in Canada. I would ask the government to reflect on that debate, quietly go through Hansard and look at that exchange. The worst predictions of that debate came true. I wish that had not happened.
The minister is to be commended for taking a strong position. My Liberal colleague clearly stated that the position is of course focused on powerful political entities, and that is that the big five in the Security Council who have been the big sellers. It is tough for an independent country like Canada to walk up to the big boys and say "knock it off".
This is more than an abstract problem. Here are some of the realities we have to deal with. During the last 15 years the Middle East has taken about one-third of all arms traded globally. Thirty nations, including Canada, sold Saddam Hussein more than $50 billion worth of weapons before he attacked Kuwait. Arab nations together have spent more than $150 billion on importing arms over the last 12 years, yet not one of these countries is confident of its security.
Just reflect on what that $150 billion could have done for Third World countries, for the hungry children that
the minister properly addressed some of his comments to. Just reflect on what that money could have done.
After recently receiving $3 billion from the gulf oil states and the U.S. for its assistance in pushing Saddam Hussein from Kuwait, Syria has ordered $1 billion worth of Scuds from North Korea, all of which will be able to hit Israel. It is a serious problem.
I conclude by reading this one paragraph: "The Bush administration has backed away from earlier demands that conventional arms control be a major objective for the post-war Middle East. Washington now plans to sell $25 billion of arms to the Middle East in 1991 alone. About 67 per cent of all U.S. weapons being sold in 1991 by the United States will go to the Middle East."
That is absolute madness. If I may express an opinion to our colleagues south of the border, that is an insult to the dead who sacrificed their lives for the freedom of Kuwait, only to find that some impelling economic reasons may be putting the U.S. government in the position of rearming the very same regions.
Having said that, I wish to address myself to the chronic problem of the State of Israel and its neighbours.
I am blessed with the same amount of ignorance of the nuances of trying to find an answer to that problem.
I do not have any more knowledge or any less than any other observer, but it seems to me-and I feel strongly about it-that it should be stated, if not evident, that Israel must look to some form of negotiations to deal with its internal and external security. It must expect and can demand the same international commitment that brought together 16 diverse nations to protect the integrity of the boundaries of Kuwait. It must ask for the same commitment from international communities to protect its sovereign boundaries as well.
Until that commitment is given fully, openly, and honestly to the State of Israel by all the players, negotiations that will reach a conclusion will not be possible.
While we get hung up on the nuances of who is to be at the table, while we walk on eggs concerned about expressing opinions of who should or should not be there, the basic reassurance that must be given to force an international debate around "where to from here" is
March 15, 1991

a statement that the very commitment given by those 16 nations to protect the sovereign integrity of the borders of Kuwait must be given to protect the sovereign integrity of the borders of Israel, which were established by the United Nations the first time in history.
Having said that, I believe there will be a harvest of damage done to the western nations by the war, based on propaganda that we are not in control of. My colleague from the Liberal Party mentioned, in a very astute, brief comment, that we may have damaged our role as Canadians but still can give advice and peacekeeping.
Unfortunately I believe we have placed ourselves, through this experience, in the position of being lumped in with the rest of the western nations and of being viewed, frankly, as attempting to impose western hegemony on the region.
I hope that every effort is made by this government, and I think the minister has done it with his visit, not only to confirm the alliance but to set a distinct and separate pattern defining Canada. The minister is to be congratulated for taking this unilateral drive himself.
To separate Canada further, I would ask that this government propose a unilateral ban on the sale of arms from Canada as a demonstration backing up its position against the arms sale. A ban by Canada would be a powerful signal that we mean what we say.
My time is up and I would like to conclude with a comment concerning my constituents in the Esquimau naval base and the other military forces there. It is on record that I did not want to see this war take place. It is also on record in my speech that once the decision was made I hoped for a quick dispatch and early return. They have done us proud again. I do not like the circumstances they were placed in, but they have done us proud again. Every Canadian must feel a bit better today that we have an independent armed force that is attached directly to a parliamentary government. I thank those families and I thank those men and women who served us.
I say in conclusion I hope, like in most other wars, their service has not been in vain.

listened very closely to the minister of trade, as punishing as that may be. I thought I would address myself specifically to some of the comments he made.
The minister chose to use a columnist as the source of all of his rationale for supporting the free trade agreement. I do not know if that columnist has ever met a payroll or not, but I have chosen to respond by dealing with some of the business community that he claims are supporting the free trade agreement. I will read some of the quotes.
Let us hear them now.

No. Well, I know you are anxiously awaiting those comments. As a matter of fact, you leapt your feet, hoping that I would be given the floor to answer your concerns. And by the grace of goodness, I was.
I want to bring to the minister's attention a statement by Patrick Lavelle, the vice-president for Canadian auto parts maker, Magna International. He is not a columnist. He does not belong to the CLC. Why those gratuitous attacks on individually named people has a place in this debate, I do not know, but if that is what you choose to do, that is your decision.
I quote: "The government is becoming involved in the U.S.-Mexico negotiations for no pressing economic
reason, and with no idea of what it hopes to achieve" said Patrick Lavelle, a vice-president for Canadian auto parts maker, Magna International.
That was at a conference on free trade and the possibility of talks with Mexico. I point out to the House that if the hon. members opposite would do some research, they would see that of 140 international instruments on the environment, Mexico has ratified 27. It has adhered to the 1985 Vienna
Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer and the 1987 Montreal protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer. They passed extensive domestic legislation and environmental standards. They still have difficulties in implementation and enforcement because of their financial limitations. They are a developing country with a large foreign debt.

With respect to labour conditions-I hope this will be of interest to the hon. gentleman who has obviously done no research into this situation-Mexico has ratified 61 of more than 170 International Labour Organization conventions, including eight of what are known as the 11 core conventions, for example, freedom of association, abolition of forced labour, equal remuneration, and non-discrimination.
This compares to the United States which has ratified only seven of these ILO conventions, none of them core, and Canada which has adhered to 26, four of which are core. Mexico actually has a better record than either the United States or Canada in adhering to international conventions dealing with labour matters. States Free Trade Agreement by withdrawing from the current trade
negotiations between the United States, Mexico and Canada.
Even a year ago today few of us would have predicted that we would be in this House discussing a trilateral trade deal with Mexico. This is an issue that has come upon us very quickly but its seriousness demands that we examine our options fully. While time constraints mean that we must react quickly, we must be careful not to over-react, careful not to react with knee-jerk divisiveness.
Given that the motion before us provides an opportunity to examine the issue of a North American free trade
agreement, I welcome its introduction into the House. However, I find the substance of the motion presents great difficulty.
The motion speaks of the worsening of the social and economic hardship caused by the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I agree. The motion then goes on to prescribe a recipe to avoid the worsening of our social and economic ills, that we withdraw from this current trilateral trade negotiation.
The motion before us, given the reality of today, however harsh given the six years of Toiy rule, I believe is a flight into fantasy.
We can rightfully say that if we were in power we would not have the trade agreement we have now. We would not have signed a deal that gave away so much and brought so little. We would not have stacked the deck against Canadians, and then proceeded to strip away our ability to become better trained, better equipped, more competitive with soaring interest rates, retraining cuts, education cuts, R and D cuts, and science and technology cuts. We would not have been in the jam we are in today.
We can all indulge in "what if" in this House until we are blue in the face and until the last Canadian has stopped listening. The fact of the matter is that we are not the ruling party. The economic mismanagement that the ruling party has brought us is real and demands our attention here in the House. It will not be resolved by talking about "what if" and withdrawing from reality.
The fact of the matter is Canada is at the table. Whether we like it or not, we are stuck with this Minister for International Trade and this Prime Minister who sold out Canadians under the Canada-U.S. free trade deal. Whether we like it or not, we are stuck with this government for at least the next year and a half.
The Liberal Party has called for an election, because we feel Canadians need a new direction. The fact of the matter is that we are stuck with this government, and it is the members opposite who will be responsible for forwarding Canada's position in these negotiations. Those negotiations will go on.
Given that reality, it seems quite logical and in the best interests of all Canadians not to waste valuable time in the House of Commons on a flight into fantasy.
