In other words, the hon. member is right, people who are in industries where retraining is needed have every right to come to the provincial and federal governments and say: "What can you do to help us". We have obligations to help and we believe we are meeting them.

Madam Speaker, I have so many reactions to the hon. member's speech I am not sure where to start, so they will be random comments.
Anybody who would quote Richard Nixon and Diane Francis in the same paragraph is really reaching for people to endorse what they believe in, because that is apparently the opposite end of the spectrums or the opposite end of walks of life. But, whatever, when you are desperate you will quote just about anybody.
The member talked about us being illogical. I have been on a few committees with this gentleman as the chairman. I think he is a very reasonable man, but the problem is that the government has these ideological blinders on and it cannot react in any other way.
The only thing that I can absolutely and positively refute is his indication that the dispute panels are very successful. They fast track the decisions.
He cited the pork ruling. Of course, we have not finished with the pork ruling yet. The Americans had one last kick at it. They said: "There is some sort of extraordinary appeal that we can make." They have not given up. When they lose, we lose.
Supply
The panel dispute mechanism is not working, and I am sure the member knows that.
It is working.

It is not working.
As far as the New Democrats being protectionists and isolationists, we suggest that we go out there and negotiate deals from our strength. We should be the initiators, and not tie ourselves to the Americans. We are tied in with them, and we are losing.
They are going to grab our hand and say: "Let's go over here. We know what is good for you." Ask the people again. They know what is good for them. They say: "No. We will not accept what you did negotiate, and we are not prepared to accept what you are going to negotiate for us because we have lost control of our destiny." I know you do not want to hear it, Madam Speaker, but we are losing control of our sovereignty.
Canadians believe that because they see it happening each and every day. The member says: "We did not say this. We said this." I guess there was a varied story during the campaign because I know in my riding the member indicated to me that there were going to be thousands of jobs created in my riding, let alone across Canada.
The bottom line is we are suffering. We are in a recession. If it is not totally related to free trade, certainly the high Canadian dollar and interest rates going along with free trade are part and parcel of the Canadian problem.

Madam Speaker, yes, there is a great gulf between the member and myself.
He cannot find a single economist and analyst of what has happened in the last 18 months who does not say that the free trade agreement has restrained the negative effect of the recession on this country. Every independent analysis says that.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member laughs. The same folks who say that health care is not being funded because of free trade say that every single job loss is because of free trade.
I say to them that it is factually untrue. Everybody who is in the world of analysis of this stuff knows it. The

March 15, 1991
Supply
reason some Canadians are afraid of the free trade agreement is that members opposite keep telling them what is, in my view, factually untrue. They are saying that it is the free trade agreement that is causing the job losses.
It is not the free trade agreement that is causing the job losses. If there is a recession going on in the country because your spending policy is particularly provincial or too high and if you have governments spending beyond their means in this country and you drive interest rates up to the point where they are higher than they should be-
I want to deal first with the comments that were made on the motion of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca that we are debating today. After all, he is the one who started the debate and moved the motion that condemns the Canadian government's involvement in these discussions. I can understand why.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, in a vigorous speech this morning, went on at considerable length.
Check your 1988 election promises.
Here they go. Here they go, again. Madam Speaker, you can't tell a socialist anything anymore in this House.
Sure you can.
No, I can't. There is no point. When a wall is made of concrete, that is what it is made of.
An excellent speech.

I would not say that it was excellent but he certainly got going, talking about how the Liberal Party had lost the voice when the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra left as leader of this party. After all, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra led the fight against the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement in the 1988 election campaign, and extremely well he did too.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to be able to participate in a debate on Mexico-U.S.-Canada free trade.
This is clearly an issue that, like the free trade debate we were through two years ago with respect to the U.S. agreement, will be of considerable importance over the next period of time as we watch the government embark on these veiy important negotiations.
I am also happy to be part of a party that has come up with a very sensible forward-looking policy on free trade that acknowledges the existence of a situation that we fought valiantly against throughout the election.
Valiantly?

The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie is getting overwrought. He thinks our policy changes week by week, but in fact as he will discover in the documents I am about to quote our policy has been consistent in this matter for many months now, certainly for more than a month. The quotation I am about to get is very up-to-date and very sensible. I will come to that in a minute, if he can control himself.
The amazing thing was that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca tried to pretend that the Liberal Party had lost its direction since the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra left the leadership. I want to assure the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca that is simply not so. Of all the people to complain about it, he should be among the last. With great respect, anyone from the New Democratic Party should be the last to complain about a lack of direction in the Liberal Party with respect to free trade, because it was the members of the New Democratic Party, particularly their former leader, honest Ed Broadbent, who attacked the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra throughout the campaign. He questioned his credibility, accused him of being dishonest with the people of Canada, accused him of not being true to his view that the free trade agreement was bad for Canada.
I can remember Mr. Broadbent accusing the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra of changing his mind when he took office. He said: "When the Liberals take office they will pretend they never made a promise to tear up the free trade deal. He does not really mean it". That is what the leader of the New Democratic Party said, and the leader of the New Democratic Party joined ranks with his friend the Prime Minister of Canada and attacked the integrity of the hon. member for Vancouver
March 15, 1991

Quadra in a way that can only be described as despicable. It was a shocking disgrace.
If there is any evidence lacking of that little pact between the Prime Minister and Mr. Broadbent, we can only look at Mr. Broadbent's nose in the trough today, at the job he has been given by the Prime Minister, his $120,000 a year salary and the concomitant pension. He is doing very well, thank you.
I think it is one of the most disgraceful political episodes we have had in this country, when the Prime Minister and the former leader of the New Democratic Party joined ranks and attacked the member for Vancouver Quadra and said that what he said was not true. They attacked his credibility throughout the election campaign and undermined it. In the result they were successful in keeping their own fortunes high enough to ensure a defeat of the Liberal Party at the polls and the victory of a government that was pledged to bring the free trade agreement into effect, and that is exactly what they did.
Hon. members on my left sat here in the House with me in December 1988, voting against this agreement, knowing that their leader had helped to undermine the credibility of the principal champion of the fight against free trade, namely the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, and assuring a Conservative victory that brought us this dreadful agreement that has cost Canadians so many jobs, as we heard this morning.
For the hon. member from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca to stand here and rant and rave as he did about Liberal hypocrisy was just a bit much. It is a shame he is not here to defend himself on these outrageous comments, because really it was an absolutely shocking performance.
It is a shame that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is not here.
It is too bad the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is not here, or he would have things to say on this particular debate as well.
I will bet he could.

I want to turn to the Minister for International Trade who got up and huffed and puffed about the comments made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. To describe his speech as a lot of huff and puff is perhaps kind and probably the only
Supply
thing one could say about it. As the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie pointed out, it was long on humour but short on facts.
In listening to the minister, one has to wonder exactly what it is he is proposing to do in these talks with Mexico and the United States concerning free trade. That is the concern we in this party have about the whole approach the government is taking to this agreement.
What is its approach? We have never been told. We certainly got no enlightenment this morning from the Minister for International Trade who participated in the debate. One would have thought that instead of reading from Maclean's magazine, Royal Bank projections and economic reports, he might have got down to some facts and told us what the government's position is in these negotiations. We did not get any of that at all.
The minister quoted Diane Francis as though she was some expert who knew everything about the effects of the old free trade agreement. He told us nothing about Canada's proposals in this new round of negotiations in which we are about to take part.
I must say that Diane Francis may be an expert. I do not know her qualifications in this field, but when I read her articles I have doubts that she knows what she is talking about on the subject of free trade. She seems to think that none of the job losses that have occurred in Canada over the last two years are the result of free trade. Yet the Prime Minister himself throughout the election campaign in 1988 assured us that once this deal was approved there were going to be hundreds of thousands of jobs created for Canadians; it was going to become a period of uninterrupted prosperity and increasing wealth for Canadians.
We all know that we are now in the worst recession we have had in the last decade, since the early 1980s. We know unemployment has gone to its highest level since the government took office in 1984. We know that interest rates have gone way back up and recently down because of the government's ham-fisted policies of mucking up the Canadian economy. Hundreds of thousands of jobs have been lost, not created. We have unemployment of 1.4 million people in Canada today.
All this, we are told, is not the fault of the free trade agreement. This is just a recession or something that is

March 15, 1991
Supply
apparently caused by external forces, according to the government. Of course we know differently. We know that the government's policies have caused this recession: the high interest rate policy, the tight money policy, the overspending policy of the government in its management of the fiscal affairs of the country. I could go on and on.
The government itself has to accept responsibility for the economic mess we are in, yet it does not want to blame it on the free trade agreement. It has at least managed to avoid that because it would be so contradictory to what it was saying throughout the campaign in 1988.
I cannot help but believe that many of the jobs are lost as a result of the free trade deal. I can point to examples in my own riding of factories that have closed down and moved to the United States.
Hon. members can say it was not because of the free trade deal. That is what we always hear from the minister and people like the hon. member for Don Valley West. They say that there is no evidence that ties it to the free trade deal. I have evidence. When the president of the company says that with free trade there is no advantage to staying in Canada and that he is closing down and moving south, and moves, and all the people are laid off, what more evidence do we need?
Hon. members opposite persist in denying that there is any evidence that free trade has hurt Canada. I say that there is evidence that it has hurt Canada. There is very little evidence that it has helped Canada. Their own policies may be solely responsible for the recession, but they are not admitting that. So what else is responsible? I suggest the free trade agreement has not brought the promised bonanza to Canada but in fact has helped make this recession worse.
It was obvious to everyone when the deal was negotiated that there would be certain businesses and industries that would close down in Canada as a result of free trade. Those are closing lock, stock and barrel, and we are losing jobs in Canada as a direct result of this agreement.
Unfortunately the minister will not stand up and admit that fact in the House. He will not give us figures, and his department does not even prepare them. They do not even look at the facts and attempt to give Canadians a
fair, balanced and honest picture of what this deal has done for this country.
Surely before we embark on another round of negotiations with someone else, we should have some figures on this, some authoritative figures, not Diane Francis' quotations in Maclean's magazine. Let us get some facts on it. I would ask the minister to produce some hard figures from myriad experts he has working in his department who now probably are being pulled off this kind of work to deal with the situation, with the Mexico talks.
I would like to quote an authority on this. I refer to a member of this House, a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, the member for Etobicoke North, who is well-known for his extensive views and writing on free trade. I have some words from him now. He expresses the fear-
He is well-known for supporting the GST.
He supported the GST.
The hon. member wants me to speak about the birds and the bees. I am sticking to the Mexico-Canada free trade agreement.
We want something different.

The hon. member is a well-known authority. He has expressed his concern about the government's ability to negotiate for this country, a concern that many of us have felt for years. We have the record of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, which was so badly bungled by the government. Then we have the record of Meech Lake, which was botched and botched again by this government. It is understandable that Canadians are nervous when they hear that this government is going to go out and negotiate another deal.
To say the least.

"To say the least", as my hon. colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception says.
The hon. member for Etobicoke North, who is the trade critic for this party, expressed his grave concern as follows:
-the same government that so mishandled United States-Canada free trade is now embarking on the negotiation of free trade among the United States, Canada and Mexico. Canadians have no
March 15, 1991

confidence in the Mulroney Government's ability to protect Canadian interests given its failure to promote Canada's interests during the United States-Canada free trade negotiations.
Truer words were never spoken.
I go on to quote the hon. member:
The lesson that Canadians learned from those negotiations is that the Government's promises of adjustment assistance are empty promises. Nor has this Government instituted the necessary educational and retraining programs to assist Canadians to be more competitive. Worse still, its high interest rate, high dollar monetary policy has crippled Canadian business in the face of increased competition from the United States.
Those are words that I suggest are far more relevant to the debate today than the quotations from Diane Francis in Maclean's magazine the minister cited in support of his arguments. I urge the minister to read the hon. member for Etobicoke North's statements on this subject. I could go on quoting him at great length, but he is not the only one who is concerned about the government's ability to negotiate.
Let me read from one of the supporters of free trade who has given us the benefit of his views. It is reported in today's edition of Le Devoir.

The article is in French and reports what the vicepresident of Samson, Belair, Deloitte and Touche International had to say. The vice-president of the firm, Mr. Pierre S. Pettigrew, indicated his concern about the ability of this government to negotiate an agreement with Mexico. This is what the author of the article, Michel Van de Walle of Canadian Press, reported, and I quote:
A supporter of free trade, Mr. Pettigrew was very critical of the way the Mulroney government conducted negotiations with the United States. He said that negotiations were very unsatisfactory in the furniture sector, for instance. Canada had agreed to reduce its tariffs at the same rate as the Americans. That was crazy. Our tariffs were twice as high as the U.S. tariffs. This meant that we had to reduce a tariff of 16 per cent over five years, while the U.S. tariff was 5 per cent to start with. It shows a total lack of respect for our industry.

Canadians from every walk of life, supporters or not of the free trade agreement, are concerned about this government's ability to negotiate a fair and reasonable agreement that protects Canada's interests. Yet the government has indicated that it is marching off to negotiate this deal.
Supply
We in the Liberal Party are very concerned that we are not getting from the government a clear statement of its intentions. We call on the government today, under the guise of this motion moved by the member of the New Democratic Party, to come clean and tell Canadians what goals we can expect from these talks. What are the national objectives we should have in going into these discussions? What benefits does the government see as coming from these talks for Canadians? Are Canadians supportive of the government initiative in participation in the talks?
Surely we cannot decide whether it is a good thing or a bad thing for Canada unless we have some statement from the government of what we expect to get. There has been no statement forthcoming. We are simply told free trade is good, that the freer trade is the better off we are all going to be.
Canadians do not swallow that line. They should not have to swallow it. They should be given some facts and figures to back this up. We should be told, for example, what things we are likely to be able to purchase from Mexico at a lower rate after the agreement than what we can purchase today.
We should be told by our government what kinds of things we can reasonably expect to export to Mexico if its tariff barriers come down. Yet not a scintilla of evidence has been put before this House to give us some indication of what benefits or otherwise might result from a free trade agreement with that country.
It is because they don't know.
It may be because they don't know. If they don't know, surely they should find out before they start participating.
It didn't stop them before.

The hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception says it did not stop them before. He is quite right. They got into the talks with the United States as a means of finding some way out of the fact that they had done nothing in this country for four years in government and needed something to go the electorate with in 1988.
What was the result?

The hon. member for Edmonton Northwest asks: "What was the result?" As I said at the outset of my remarks, had he been paying close attention, the result would have been different had the efforts of the member for Vancouver Quadra not been so effectively

March 15, 1991
Supply
undermined by the then leader of the New Democratic Party.
The second objective the Liberal Party promotes is that we should be seeking multilateral trading relations with other countries to get us out of the very unsatisfactory bilateral trade relations that we have with the United States at this time.
Third, we believe that we should negotiate an agreement that could be extended to include other countries in the western hemisphere and possibly in Europe and on the Pacific Rim.
As a party we have always supported the concept of free trade. What we have not supported is the particular deal that this government produced which-and I do not want to go into all that again-included much more than free trade. It covered far more than trade. It included a sale of Canada's resources and the restructuring of Canada's economy to one of dependence.
Fourth, we would ask the government to outline adjustment programs for Canadian labour and for Canadian industry that will be put in place before the agreement comes into force. We were promised, during the 1988 election campaign, adjustment programs for Canadian workers and for Canadian industry after the free trade agreement became law. There have been no adjustment programs. In fact, as we have said for months in the House, there have been cuts in what programs there were in place before that might have served as adjustment programs.
There have been no new ones created. In fact the government has completely failed in delivering on that promise. It has broken its to Canadians and it has done worse than that, it has cut back on the programs that were in existence.
Fifth and finally, we would ask for some guarantee from the government that Canada's social, cultural and regional development programs will remain in place following this deal. No such undertaking was given in respect of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. We have watched this government slash and cut away at those things in Canada.
We do not have the protection in place as a result of that agreement for Canadian cultural industries that we feel are important. We hope that in considering the negotiations today we will have those programs put in
place so that when the new agreement, if any, is worked out with Mexico and the United States we will have protection for Canada's cultural industries.
Those are the points that we as a party are putting forward. We believe they are positive. We believe Canada should be involved in these talks. We support that part of the initiative. However we ask that these safeguards be put in place so that Canadians are not pillaged by their government the way they were in 1988.

Madam Speaker, at the beginning of his speech, the hon. member said that he could not judge the expertise of Diane Francis, but I simply would like to read a short paragraph from the article. Ms. Francis said: "The facts show that Canada has prospered under free trade. For the month in which free trade came into force, January 1989, Statistics Canada reported 12,436,000 jobs in this country. In November, November 1990, the most recent date for which figures are available, there were 12,497,000 jobs, a net gain of 63,000 jobs in this country".
In another paragraph she mentioned: "Free trade has been and still is a good economic policy". Perhaps, but her reasoning is as follows: "Because it ensures access to the best markets in the world and forces Canada to become more efficient".
Madam Speaker, although the hon. member says he doesn't know Ms. Francis, I would like to hear his response to this: Between December 1989, when free trade came into force, until November 1, 1990, a net surplus of 63,000 jobs was created in this country. Although I hope he will not confuse a recession with a free trade agreement that gives us access to the best markets in the world, I would like to hear the hon. member's response, to be able to judge his comments on what Ms. Francis said.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it isn't easy to answer the hon. member's question as stated, because he quoted figures indicating the number of Canadians on the labour market for two months only: January 1989 and November 1990. The problem is this: During that period, people immigrated to Canada. We admitted more than 250,000 people from other countries during that period. The hon. member referred to an increase of 60,000 in the number of people
March 15, 1991

with jobs. Sixty thousand is not much, considering that 250,000 new arrivals came to this country. It is not the same thing. According to the Prime Minister, free trade was supposed to create several thousand jobs, 125,000 jobs in this country. Where are those jobs? And what does 63,000 represent? It is not enough, and I am sure the hon. member will agree.
I have another quote, Madam Speaker, by my colleague, the hon. member for Etobicoke North, which might be of interest to the hon. member for Saint-Jean. He said, and I quote:
The Mulroney government allows the priorities of Mexico and the United States to take precedence. That is not the position Canada should have taken. We should have aimed at a global and multilateral expansion of our economy in the western hemisphere, instead of a slow trickle.
That is a very important point. I hope the hon. member for Saint-Jean will be able to inform the Tory caucus of the excellent ideas put forward by the hon. member for Etobicoke North.

I listened to the member for Kingston and the Islands very carefully, and a lot of what he said today kind of re-fought the last election campaign. He indicated that the party he represents in this House was the major opposition to the trade deal with the United States.
It seems to me that what we are hearing today from the Liberal members in this House is that they are speaking on both sides of this issue. It is getting increasingly difficult to make any sense out of what they are saying.
I want to ask the member if he would give us a straightforward answer on just exactly where his party stands today on the trade deal with the United States, on an expanded trade deal including Mexico and the conditions in Mexico, which he seems to be somewhat aware of.
He talked about the previous leader of his party and that it was the fight of his life for the member from Vancouver Quadra. I want the member to understand that the fight is still going on. Many of us are still fighting the fight of someone else's life, and I wonder where the member from Vancouver Quadra is on this issue and why is he not continuing the fight of his life.
Supply

Why the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby would ask me what the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is saying or what he thinks on this issue is beyond me. I have not asked him. I would have thought that as a near neighbour she might pop into Vancouver one of these days and ask him herself.
I can tell the hon. member though, that if she has any trouble believing my facts with respect to the election campaign-and she seems to be a little incredulous-I urge her to read Rick Salutin's book. I have been reading it now for some weeks. He is not a particular supporter of this party. I read it at bedtime and I find it a very fine thing to help me get to sleep.
The hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby might profit from reading this book. It certainly describes the woefully inadequate attitude of her party and its leadership in the fight against free trade during the 1988 election campaign, and their attempts to discredit the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, whose view she is so interested in today.
I urge her to write to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra if she wishes to have the benefit of his opinions, and get them.
Now let me turn to the second part of her question because she seemed not to understand the Liberal position. I thought she was listening to my speech and I am sure she listened to the speech of the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk, who made an excellent presentation and presented the views of this party with clarity and precision.
I tried to be equally clear. I said during my speech that we support the government's initiative in participating in these talks because we recognize that Canada cannot afford to let this government-or, frankly, I would prefer this government were not doing the talks because we realize the risks there are in having it do it-but, unfortunately, it is the Government of Canada so somebody has to be at that negotiating table. We should not leave this to the United States and to Mexico to do on their own; we need to be involved in the talks.
I have just given a five-point outline of things we believe this government should do before it gets involved. That is, come forward with the pros and the cons; tell Canadians the advantages and disadvantages of free trade with Mexico; tell us about its objectives in going into these discussions; guarantee the protection of Canada's social programs; outline comprehensive adjustment programs for Canadian labour and industry before we

Supply
get the agreement into force, and tell us what those are going to be in advance; and, finally, negotiate an agreement that will allow more countries than the three of us to be involved in a free trade economic zone.
Those are the objectives I believe the government should pursue in this matter. That is the position of this party. I think it is perfectly clear. I hope the hon. member does not need me to put it in writing. If so, I will underline the relevant portions of my speech in Hansard on Monday and send it to her.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 5 the Prime Minister, along with Presidents Bush and Salinas, made an historic announcement, that our three countries would negotiate a North American free trade agreement.
This announcement set in train a process that will help to build and enrich our three countries.
It is not a perfect agreement, but an excellent agreement and one that is working to the mutual benefit of both Canada and the United States. As its benefits become clear to Canadians, it will be seen by all sides to be a far-sighted agreement.
February 5 is a particularly important day to me. It is my birthday, so having an analysis on that day means something special to me, especially at my advanced age.
I want to try to take a little different tack on this debate because it is back and forth-you said this and I said that, who said something in the election? I want to put another slant on it, if I can.
The Gross National Product of United States of America is $5 trillion. That is double the Gross National Product of Japan and 25 per cent of the Gross National Product of the developed world.
What we have done with the free trade agreement is open a $5 trillion market to Canadian business. Over a period of 10 years, it will become tariff free.
It is all very well for academics and others who have never had a callus on their hands to stand in this place and debate matters of trade, international affairs and so forth, but I do not know if any of them have really
operated a business or been responsible for the development or expansion of a business, or had to go out of the country to find customers because of our small population.
We have some excellent industries in Canada, and some of them have developed some substantial markets overseas. I notice that Mexico is our second largest customer for steel. We ship steel bar into Mexico. Mexico makes it into springs and ship it back into Brampton where we make automobiles. We sell the bulk of the tin plate that is used in the canning industry in Mexico, so we have a stake in that market already.
Aside from that, the argument here today seems to revolve around numbers. Who are the winners? Who are the losers? The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands looks upon the free trade agreement as some sort of balance. We did not gain any jobs, all we have done is lose jobs. He speaks of the jobs that have gone out of his constituency.
It is important to realize that this agreement is two years old. There are adjustments going on, and I will give you a perfect example.
A gentleman who happened to be the president of Toledo Scales called my office one morning and he said: "I have good news and bad news." I said: "Give me the bad news first, and I can end up with the good news." He said: "I have a plant in Windsor that we opened in 1890. We make scales, and I am going to close that plant down."
I said: "What is the good news?" He said: "I have more bad news," and I said: "What is that?" He said: "I have a head office in Mississauga, and I am going to close that down." I asked him whether there could be any good news after that. He said: "Oh yes, we are going to open a state of the art plant in Burlington,"-my constituency-"where we will combine our manufacturing and our head office in one operation. We will be world competitive. We will even be able to compete with the Japanese."
That is the type of adjustment that is going on in this country, and people do not realize it. When you sign a free trade agreement, you cannot turn things around that fast. People have to make decisions. Humans are involved.
March 15, 1991

In the case of Toledo Scales, it looked at the age of the people involved in the industry and said: "The bulk of them went on retirement." They had been there for years. It was one of those kinds of companies.
The person running an industry look at himself and asks: "What am I going to do? Am I going to stay in the domestic market? Am I going to stay in the Canadian market? Am I going to find a niche in the American market? Am I going to go North American? Am I going to go global?" Those are the decisions that a businessman has to make.
Depending on what decision he makes, he says: "I need more capital. I need more plant space. I need some more productive machinery," or, "I am going to sell this business because I am at an age when I do not want to go into the expansionist phase."
Those are decisions he has to make. The only connection to free trade is that the government has opened up this tremendous $5 trillion market and the man has an option he never had before. He has to decide just where he is going to go and how he is going to do it.
In Windsor, Dofasco, NKK of Japan, National Steel of the United States have put together a new plant to galvanize sheet steel on one side and supply it to the stamping industry that feeds the automobile industry. In other words, the galvanizing is to eliminate the rusting out of automobiles. That is being put together right now. The factory is being built and the machinery will be coming in. It is going to hire about 1,000 people. The 300 odd people left Toledo Scale, and now there will be 1,000 in place of 300, so it balances out that way.
I will give hon. members some investment dollar figures so they will get an idea.

I am not disturbed about the Mexico-Canada-U.S. suggested trade link. To me, it is an opportunity for us to look at a larger market again. I think it would be foolish if we were not there.
I agree with my friend from Kingston and the Islands that it would be foolhardy for Canada to sit on the sidelines and allow a negotiation to go on between the Mexicans and the Americans involving trade and not be there to see what is going on.
I support the initiative announced on February 5, my birthday, by the Prime Minister, President Bush and President Salinas of Mexico. I believe it will be an historic event when this comes across.

Madam Speaker, I would first like to commend the member of Parliament for Haldimand-Norfolk, who has been leading the response on behalf of the Liberal Party and the Liberal caucus in his capacity as a critic in the area of international trade.
I am also pleased to be given the opportunity to debate an opposition day motion put forward by the New Democratic Party, our friends to our left. I am wondering, however, how valuable it is to have a motion that basically fantasizes where the New Democratic Party would like the government to be. We can always get involved in a debate on whether the government should or should not take a seat at the trade talks between Mexico and the United States. However, I think they are a bit late on that, very similar to the last election, Madam Speaker, as you no doubt will recall as you were in the trenches fighting for your re-election. We recall the hesitation in which the New Democratic Party fought that particular campaign. Among the multitude of issues in that federal election obviously the one major issue that dominated all other issues was whether the Canadian government ought to pursue a free trade arrangement with the United States.
At the opening press conference the former Leader of the New Democratic Party did not even mention the two words "free trade". We all know what happened to the New Democratic Party during that campaign. Obviously we were not successful, as evidenced by where we are sitting, however let it be said that when we objected to

Supply
the agreement that was signed between our two countries we said it loudly, forcefully, clearly, and we put it squarely to Canadians. It was not a case of: "Well, we are not sure, perhaps we will talk about child care as well, maybe we will talk about this or that."
The New Democratic Party, following the last election, had a post-mortem review and the party was found to be wanting in many of the New Democratic Party's natural constituencies.
We do not need a lecture on where the party stands or stood. I think Canadians were testimony to the type of temperament that the New Democratic Party lent to the free trade debate in 1988. Now it comes with an opposition day motion. Perhaps there is great intent, perhaps there is genuine intent, but there is a lot of academic intent as well. The debate should not be "should they or should they not be" because Canadians are expecting their politicians to be discussing not flights of fantasy but flights of reality.
Whether we like it or not this government has made the decision to place itself at the table. Rather than engage Canadians in what could have been or perhaps even what should have been, I think Canadians want to be engaged in: "Okay, now that we are at the table New Democratic Party, Liberal Party, Conservative Party, what is it that Canada should be saying from its seat? What is it that Canada should be saying to the Americans and to the Mexicans who will be negotiating around that long table?" That is worth debate in this Chamber.
I would like to correct a few things, because during the course of the debate we have heard members from various sides say: "You're not in favour of freer trade". "You didn't want to go to the table". "You wanted to go under the table". The NDP say that I want to pull the chair out.
The party of which I am very proud to be a member historically has been a party that has always favoured freer trade. If there were times in our history when political parties were very much opposed to opening the road of trade between the countries of the world community, it was clearly the Conservative Party. History does not lie. Therefore, our party has always found itself trying to reform, to open, and to liberalize, in the best sense of the word, trade. We regard trade to a certain degree as the lifeblood of this country, as an encouragement to stimulate the economy and jobs.
Where we distinguish ourselves from our hon. friends on the other side is the type of agreement that we would want to enter into with the United States of America or with another country. Therefore, the distinguishing feature should not be that this party was against freer trade but that this party fought with no apologies in 1988, led admirably by our former leader, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, for a very different kind of agreement. The type of agreement they had put their signature to was an agreement that we hoped would not materialize. Unfortunately, as we look across the land we see that our prognosis was correct, as we try to see, in the aftermath of free trade, where the success stories are.
The members on the other side pointed to "All the Fallen Sparrows", that was a quote used by one of my colleagues. Listening to the hon. member who spoke before me, the member for Burlington, when he referred to some factory making cookies, you would figure that every cookie that gets baked is because of free trade. That is an argument we should discount pretty readily. Therefore, we ought to be taking a look at what the adjustment has been after the trade agreement that was signed by the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States.
I am hard pressed to see where the success stories have been. I am hard pressed to believe that it has helped us more than it has hurt us. I see, in my own backyard in Toronto, that not every job that is lost can be blamed on or pinned simply on the free trade agreement.
I have talked to many businessmen, I have had calluses on my hands when I worked in construction putting myself through university, I am also the son of a Canadian who owns a small business himself. I am able to meet, as I have, with business interests in my community and outside my community of York West, and I am trying with those Canadians to see how free trade has encouraged a greater number of jobs, encouraged greater expansion of our industry. It has done the opposite in the grand scheme, whether in the case of energy, in the case of manufacturing, in the case of furniture, or in the case of many industries that I have in my own industrial parkland in York West. It was supposed to be a bonanza, it was supposed to be a Messiah for the creation of thousands upon thousands of jobs, for the American firms to come here and build their factories. Instead, what we have become is a warehouse economy.
March 15, 1991

The Americans do not have to come to our country and build factories to produce products and therefore create jobs; they are not doing that. What are they doing in some of their industries? What they are doing in the States where they have their plants is augmenting their production by a number of hours, they produce incredible quantities of those goods, then they ship them to Canada where they rent a warehouse and we become truck drivers. We become distributors of products under that free trade regime. Where are the job spin-offs in Canada? Certainly not in the truck industry. They are being produced in the States, where they are augmenting the number of hours and production lines to meet the Canadian market.
Where is the research and development in driving trucks and in setting up warehouses? There is none. Where is the wealth creation that we spoke about, that we were promised? Instead, those industries that cannot compete with the Americans, which cannot possibly compete with the economies of scale, flowing against logic, are going out of business. They are beginning to downsize. They are beginning to consider going south of the border. That is a reality that has been bom in the advent of the so-called free trade Messiah between our two countries.
Who speaks for the workers 45, 50, 55 years of age when a plant closes because it says it cannot compete any longer? What does the hon. member for Burlington and other members of Parliament who face such people in their constituencies tell the person who is 55 and has worked 30 years in a plant which all of a sudden gets shut down? No one wants to invest in a 55-year-old, or not readily so, despite a wealth of experience.
That 55-year old Canadian still may have a mortgage to pay, still may have kids going through university, still may be required to work another five, to seven, to ten years to make ends meet. What do we tell a worker after this Prime Minister promised the country during the last election that he and his government would deliver the best transition programs the world has ever known?
Another broken promise.

It is not only a broken promise, but it is absolutely unacceptable and irresponsible to say those

things without fulfilling those promises. Men and women who are displaced at least had a hope that if things were going to go wrong in the free trade agreement, if there were firms and industries and sectors of our economy that were not going to be able to compete as well or as strong with the Americans, at least had a glimmer of hope that there would somehow be some catch, some adjustment program, some capacity to take them and say: "Look, under the free trade agreement your business or sector did not have the technology, did not have the manpower, did not have the know-all to compete. That firm or sector is going to fall, but we are going to take you and employ you in this other industry".
On the one hand, we do not have the economic wealth being generated that was promised. On the other hand, we have unemployed workers across this country who are hurting and hurting badly.
It is also not solely free trade. It is a comprehensive situation facing the Canadian economy and the Canadian worker in that Canadian economy. We could combine the advent of free trade that has hurt us more than it has helped us. One of the reasons I question our friends in the New Democratic Party so that perhaps there are two options to that table with Mexico. Their option is not to be there, even though the government said it will be, but the other option if we are there is to stop the misery that they speak of in their motion which says:
This House calls upon the government to avoid a worsening of the
social and economic hardship-
My preferred option is to give the Government of Canada a set of marching orders to utilize at that table, to reopen the existing agreement between the United States and Canada, and to say to our friends on the government benches that we are hurting and we are hurting badly in these sectors; that now they have a golden opportunity, as our trade critic has said, to reopen the deal and revisit energy, for instance.
Who in their right mind would treat Americans as Canadians in times of energy crisis? Show me one country that has agreements of that magnitude in terms of energy self-sufficiency, and I will sit down in my place. There is not one country that would give away its energy to another country and treat it as it would its own citizens and its own economy.

Supply
I find it completely irresponsible for a Canadian government to treat American sources as its own nationals. That is a giveaway. However, what I am suggesting is perhaps we can convince them to reopen them. How do we reopen it if we are not at the table? How do we revisit something if no one is talking, no one is debating, and no one is negotiating? How would they suggest that the misery stop, if we don't try to ask this government to use the occasion to tell the Americans that on a number of fronts we would like to cross the t's and dot the i's in a very different way?
When the question of the free trade agreement is put together, we also have to add to the equation of our economy the question of high interest rates, the question of our high Canadian dollar, the question that we are now going through a very bad recession that makes the 1981-82 period virtually a cakewalk with whomever we speak to. The real cost of interest rates now are higher costs. The difference between American interest rates and Canadian interest rates in 1982 was negligible; right now there is a differential.
In 1981 and 1982 Canadians were still working. Ask people in the construction industry, ask people in our trades industry, ask people in the housing market, ask whomever you wish, wherever they are, a very simple question, whether this recession is worse than the one in 1981-82 which happened to be an international one, unlike this "made-in-Canada" recession, especially by Tories.
Tell that to first-time buyers who are finally getting into the Toronto market.

It is nice to have the members opposite awake finally. It took us six hours but they are finally awake.
The final variable, or another one, is also the question of the tax structure in this country, the question of the GST. When we begin to put all those variables together, is it any wonder that we are in a recession? Is it any wonder that the economy slowly but surely and gradually and consistently is being strangled?
To make matters worse, we just came off the heels of a budget some three weeks ago. Did the budget offer inspiration? Did the budget offer some employment stimulus? Did the budget try to inspire a nation out of
the pit of recession into which it was placed by this government?
The Minister of Finance always gets up and says: "Oh, boy, when those Liberals were in government during 1981-82 they threw money at their problems".
We had good government then.

We did not throw money at our problems. The government of 1981-82 recognized that we were living through an international recession. Rather than do nothing, as this government advocates in its budget, the government of the time created labour intensive and capital works programs.
Why? Because it tried to assist its citizens to survive and live through the recession of 1981-82. Then we had unprecedented growth in 1984-85-86-87.
What does the government do in its recession that it got us into? The responsibility of a government is to say: "If we have to spend a few dollars to help Canadians get back to work, if we can inject some inspiration into the economy, if we can kick-start the engine, then we are a government that is showing leadership".
Where is the leadership of a government that throws the country into a recession and then pulls a Pontius Pilate and says: "We can't spend. If you are hurting we feel bad, but we can't do anything about it"?
Canadians deserve better. Canadians would want us to try to inject the economy with some stimulus, because if we are stimulated as an economy then the revenues come back. If no one is working, if plants are closing two to three weeks at a time, if they are downsizing, if Canadians are walking the streets unemployed and we are paying UIC, when will we come out of our recession? When will we put Canadians back to work? When are factories going to hum again? When are we going to get the 24-hour cycles again in factories?
We won't, as long as this government persists in taking the stand of simply backing off the problems rather than trying to help Canadians survive the dark times.
Yes, there will be good times again. We need to recognize that. There are cycles, but let us help Canadians during the down cycles and then reap the fruits of their labour during the good cycles.

Madam Speaker, just a very quick question.
The hon. member referred to a budget three weeks ago that he thought was extremely regressive. Last week, we saw the province of Newfoundland and its Liberal premier come out with a budget that seemed to follow the same types of spending controls as exhibited by the finance minister. I would like the hon. member to explain to me how that Liberal government's budget is going to turn things around when he also seems to recognize that there is a tremendous debt burden.
Would the hon. member please explain to Canadians why Premier Wells, a hero across Canada, is taking a tough stand just like this federal government.

Madam Speaker, first, let me say two things.
Premier Wells, in his own riding, is much more popular than the Prime Minister. Second, if the gentleman was somewhat more honest, he would have also told Canadians that the budget of Newfoundland came after a federal budget that basically slashed and passed on the deficit reduction to the provinces.
We were not surprised. We said, on the night of the budget, through our finance critic, Mr. Gray, the hon. member for Windsor West, through our Deputy Leader, Ms. Copps, the hon. member for Hamilton East, and through subsequent speakers, that when the government talks in the federal budget about deficit reduction, when it talks about the medicare system and the cutbacks that it would be pushing the problem to the top.

On a point of order, Madam Speaker, I believe the hon. member called my hon. friend here dishonest. I would like him to withdraw that remark.

Of course, I will give the hon. member for York West the opportunity to explain or withdraw.
I would also bring to his attention, if I may, that he has been in the House at least as long as I have been in the House. He knows that members do not refer to their colleagues by their names, but by the name of their ridings. Giving the name of their ridings after does not make the first line correct.

You are absolutely right, Madam Speaker, I should know better.
In terms of my use of the word "dishonest" I did not mean it against the hon. member at all. I withdraw that word completely and without any problem.
What I tried to point out is that the question of the Newfoundland budget was not an initiation but a response to the economic tightrope that was left after the government in Ottawa presented its budget which pushed deficit reduction on to the provinces and which cut the amounts of moneys with which provincial governments can administer their health and higher education systems.
I predict that the Government of Newfoundland will not be the only provincial government across the land to do this. That is part of the problem. We are going to see a domino effect as a result of the federal Government of Canada that has been sending the wrong signals and imposing the wrong commitments. The provincial governments will have to take care of their provincial treasuries and respond accordingly.
That is where the lack of leadership comes from. That is why it is important for a federal government to have a breadth of vision of the country it represents and leads. It has to have a sense that governments such as the Government of Newfoundland, given the difficult economic straits that it finds itself in, that every action in this place has a reaction elsewhere.
I am suggesting to the hon. member that the actions of provincial governments, be they Newfoundland or Manitoba or in other provincial capitals, when they present their budgets have the seed planted in this federal budget.
That is why we have been waging this debate in this Chamber, to try to bring the government to its senses, change its budget and do things that are going to kick-start the economy rather than continue this recession.
